beads.greek: [196] ΓΑΛΗΝΟΥ ΠΡΟς ΛΥΚΟΝ ΒΙΒΛΙΟΝ.
beads.english: [196] GALEN'S BOOK AGAINST LYCUS.

beads.greek: Ἀνεμέσητον μὲν δήπου Λύκῳ καὶ παντὶ τῷ βουληθέντι πρὸς Ἱπποκράτην γράφειν.
beads.english: It is surely no cause for reproach to Lycus, or to anyone who has wished to write against Hippocrates.

beads.greek: ἔτι δὲ ἀνεμεσητότερον οἶμαι τοῖς δυναμένοις ἀπολύσασθαι τὰ κακῶς εἰρημένα πρὸς αὐτὸν ἐγκλήματα, καθάπερ ἐν δικα στηρίῳ τοῖς ἀναγνωσομένοις ἀμφοτέρων τὰ γράμματα, τὴν ἀπολογίαν ποιήσασθαι, καὶ μάλιστα ὅταν ὁ μὲν ἐγκαλῶν πρὶν μαθεῖν τὰ λεγόμενα θρασύνεται, τῷ δ’ ἀπολογουμένῳ πεπαιδεῦσθαι κατὰ τοῦ παλαιοῦ δόγματος.
beads.english: And it is, I think, still less a cause for reproach for those who are able to refute the charges ill brought against him to make their defence, as it were in a court of law, before those who will read the writings of both parties—and especially when the accuser grows bold before he has learned what is being said, while it falls to the one making the defence to have been educated in accordance with the ancient doctrine.

greek_sentences: [196] ΓΑΛΗΝΟΥ ΠΡΟς ΛΥΚΟΝ ΒΙΒΛΙΟΝ.
Ἀνεμέσητον μὲν δήπου Λύκῳ καὶ παντὶ τῷ βουληθέντι πρὸς Ἱπποκράτην γράφειν.

ἔτι δὲ ἀνεμεσητότερον οἶμαι τοῖς δυναμένοις ἀπολύσασθαι τὰ κακῶς εἰρημένα πρὸς αὐτὸν ἐγκλήματα, καθάπερ ἐν δικα στηρίῳ τοῖς ἀναγνωσομένοις ἀμφοτέρων τὰ γράμματα, τὴν ἀπολογίαν ποιήσασθαι, καὶ μάλιστα ὅταν ὁ μὲν ἐγκαλῶν πρὶν μαθεῖν τὰ λεγόμενα θρασύνεται, τῷ δ’ ἀπολογουμένῳ πεπαιδεῦσθαι κατὰ τοῦ παλαιοῦ δόγματος.
english_sentences: [196] GALEN'S BOOK AGAINST LYCUS.
It is surely no cause for reproach to Lycus, or to anyone who has wished to write against Hippocrates.

And it is, I think, still less a cause for reproach for those who are able to refute the charges ill brought against him to make their defence, as it were in a court of law, before those who will read the writings of both parties—and especially when the accuser grows bold before he has learned what is being said, while it falls to the one making the defence to have been educated in accordance with the ancient doctrine.

beads.greek: Λύκος τοίνυν ἔγραψε [197] μὲν ἐξηγητικὰ τῶν Ἱπποκράτους ἀφορισμῶν ὑπομνήματα, λωβᾶται δὲ τοῖς δόγμασι τἀνδρὸς ἑκατέρωθεν οἷς τε ψέγειν καὶ οἷς ἐπαινεῖν τινα τῶν ἐπ’ αὐτοῦ λεγομένων οἴεται καὶ δι’ ὧν ἀντιλέγειν ἐπιχειρεῖ.
beads.english: Lycus, then, wrote [197] commentaries expounding the Aphorisms of Hippocrates, but he does violence to the man's doctrines from both sides, both in those passages in which he thinks he is censuring, and in those in which he thinks he is praising, some of the things said by him, and in those through which he attempts to contradict him.

beads.greek: τά τε γὰρ ἐπαινούμενα Λύκου φαντάσματά ἐστιν, οὐχὶ Ἱπποκράτους δόγματα, δι’ ὧν τε ἀντιλέγει δῆλός ἐστι μηδὲ τὰ στοιχεῖα τῆς Ἱπποκράτους τέχνης ἐπιστάμενος.
beads.english: For the things he praises are phantasms of Lycus, not doctrines of Hippocrates, and in the things by which he contradicts him he is manifestly ignorant even of the elements of the Hippocratic art.

beads.greek: ὅτῳ δ’ οὐκ ἔστι τῶν στοιχείων ἐπιστήμη, σχολῇ γ’ ἂν οὗτος οὐ τὰς συλλαβὰς εἰδείη τῆς τέχνης ἐκείνης ἢ τῶν ἀπ’ αὐτῆς.
beads.english: And he who has no knowledge of the elements would scarcely know the syllables of that art, or of what derives from it.

beads.greek: εἰ μὲν οὖν ἐγὼ πρῶτος ἢ μόνος ἔλεγον ἐκ θερμοῦ καὶ ψυχροῦ καὶ ὑγροῦ καὶ ξηροῦ τὰ τῶν ζώων σώματα συγκεῖσθαι νομίζειν Ἱπποκράτην, τάχα ἂν ἴσως εὐλαβέστερον ἐνεκάλουν Λύκῳ πρὶν γνῶναι τὰ στοιχεῖα τῆς Ἱπποκράτους τέχνης ἐπιχειροῦντι τῶν συγγραμμάτων αὐτοῦ γράφειν ἐξηγήσεις.
beads.english: Now if I were the first or the only one to say that Hippocrates holds the bodies of animals to be composed of hot, cold, wet and dry, perhaps I would be more cautious in charging Lycus with undertaking to write expositions of his treatises before knowing the elements of the Hippocratic art.

beads.greek: οὔτε γὰρ ὅσοι δόγμασιν ἐναντίοις ἐνεγράφησαν οὔθ’ ὅσοι μήτε τὰ πρῶτα γινώσκουσι τῆς τέχνης χρήσιμα εὔλογον ἐξηγεῖσθαι τοὺς ἀφορισμοὺς, ἀλλ’ ὥσπερ μεμαθήκασι μὲν ἐκ τῆς παιδικῆς ἡλικίας, ἐπαινοῦσι δὲ πάλιν ἢ ψέγουσιν αὐτοῦ τὰ δόγματα.
beads.english: For it is not reasonable that either those who have been enrolled under opposing doctrines, or those who do not even know the first useful things of the art, should expound the Aphorisms; but, as though they had learned them from childhood, they praise or again censure his doctrines.

english_sentences: Lycus, then, wrote [197] commentaries expounding the Aphorisms of Hippocrates, but he does violence to the man's doctrines from both sides, both in those passages in which he thinks he is censuring, and in those in which he thinks he is praising, some of the things said by him, and in those through which he attempts to contradict him.
For the things he praises are phantasms of Lycus, not doctrines of Hippocrates, and in the things by which he contradicts him he is manifestly ignorant even of the elements of the Hippocratic art.
And he who has no knowledge of the elements would scarcely know the syllables of that art, or of what derives from it.

Now if I were the first or the only one to say that Hippocrates holds the bodies of animals to be composed of hot, cold, wet and dry, perhaps I would be more cautious in charging Lycus with undertaking to write expositions of his treatises before knowing the elements of the Hippocratic art.

For it is not reasonable that either those who have been enrolled under opposing doctrines, or those who do not even know the first useful things of the art, should expound the Aphorisms; but, as though they had learned them from childhood, they praise or again censure his doctrines.

beads.greek: [198] Λύκος δὲ εἰς τοσοῦτον ἄρα τῆς Ἱπποκράτους τέχνης ἀμαθής ἐστιν, ὡς ἐγὼ θεοὺς ἅπαντας ἐπόμνυμι, τὰς πρώτας τῶν εἰς τοὺς ἀφορισμοὺς ὑπομνημάτων αὐτοῦ ἐξηγήσεις ἀναγνοὺς, οὐκέθ’ ὑπέμεινα τὸ λοιπὸν τοῦ βιβλίου ἀναγνῶναι, τοσοῦτον ἐφαίνετο τῆς γνώμης ἁμαρτάνειν τοῦ παλαιοῦ.
beads.english: [198] But Lycus, as it turns out, is so ignorant of the Hippocratic art that—I swear by all the gods—having read the first expositions of his commentaries on the Aphorisms, I could no longer bear to read the rest of the book, so far did he seem to miss the meaning of the ancient.

beads.greek: τῶν ἑταίρων δέ τινος ἀξιώσαντος ἐπακοῦσαί με τῶν εἰς τόνδε τὸν ἀφορισμὸν ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ γεγραμμένων, ἐν ᾧ φησι τὰ αὐξανόμενα πλεῖστον ἔχει τὸ ἔμφυτον θερμὸν, εἶτα πολλῶν καὶ ἄλλων παρακαλεσάντων ἀπολογήσασθαι πρὸς τὰς κατηγορίας, οὕτως ἀναγκασθεὶς ἐπὶ τόνδε τὸν λόγον ἧκον.
beads.english: But when one of my companions asked me to listen to what had been written by him on this aphorism, in which he says that growing things have the most innate heat, and then many others too urged me to make a defence against the accusations, I was thus compelled and came to this discourse.

beads.greek: Ἵνα δὲ τοῖς μὲν ὑπ’ ἐκείνου λεγομένοις, ὑπ’ ἐμοῦ δὲ μέλλουσι πρὸς αὐτὰ ῥηθῆναι, ῥᾷον ἀκολουθήσωσιν οἱ δικάσοντες ἡμῖν, ἀναγκαῖον ἔσται μοι βραχέα προειπεῖν.
beads.english: And so that those who are to judge between us may more easily follow both what is said by him and what is about to be said by me in reply to it, it will be necessary for me to say a few things by way of preface.

english_sentences: [198] But Lycus, as it turns out, is so ignorant of the Hippocratic art that—I swear by all the gods—having read the first expositions of his commentaries on the Aphorisms, I could no longer bear to read the rest of the book, so far did he seem to miss the meaning of the ancient.

But when one of my companions asked me to listen to what had been written by him on this aphorism, in which he says that growing things have the most innate heat, and then many others too urged me to make a defence against the accusations, I was thus compelled and came to this discourse.

And so that those who are to judge between us may more easily follow both what is said by him and what is about to be said by me in reply to it, it will be necessary for me to say a few things by way of preface.

beads.greek: ὅτι μέν ἐστι θερμὸν ἐν ἡμῖν ἐναργῶς ἅπασι φαίνεται, πότερα δ’ ἐκ κινήσεως τοῦτο τῆς κατὰ τὴν καρδίαν καὶ τὰς ἀρτηρίας ἔχει τὴν γένεσιν ἢ καθάπερ αὐτὸ τὸ κινεῖσθαι [199] τῇ καρδίᾳ σύμφυτον ὑπάρχει, τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον καὶ ἡ θερμασία, διαπεφώνηται τοῖς ἰατροῖς.
beads.english: That there is heat in us is evidently apparent to all; but whether this has its origin from the motion in the heart and the arteries, or whether, just as motion itself [199] is innate in the heart, in the same way the heat is too, is a matter of dispute among physicians.

beads.greek: ἀλλ’ ὅστις γε βούλεται μαθεῖν ἐπιστημονικῶς, ἀρχὰς τοῖς ζώοις ἅπασι γενέσεως εἶναι τὸ θερμὸν καὶ τὸ ψυχρὸν καὶ τὸ ξηρὸν καὶ τὸ ὑγρὸν, ἓν ἔχει βιβλίον ὑπ’ ἐμοῦ γεγραμμένον, ἐν ᾧ τὴν Ἱπποκράτους γνώμην ἐξηγοῦμαι καὶ ἀποδεικνύω.
beads.english: But whoever wishes to learn in a scientific manner that the principles of generation for all animals are the hot, the cold, the dry and the wet has one book written by me, in which I expound and demonstrate the opinion of Hippocrates.

beads.greek: τοῦτο μὲν δὴ τὸ βιβλίον ἐπιγέγραπται περὶ τῶν καθ’ Ἱπποκράτους στοιχείων.
beads.english: This book is entitled On the Elements according to Hippocrates.

beads.greek: ἕτερα δὲ ἐφεξῆς ἐστιν αὐτοῦ τὰ περὶ κράσεων, ἐν οἷς δείκνυμι τίνα μὲν τῶν σωμάτων πλείονα μοῖραν ἐν ἑαυτοῖς ἔχει τοῦ θερμοῦ στοιχείου, τίνα δ’ ἐλάττονα.
beads.english: And following it there are others, those On Mixtures, in which I show which bodies have in themselves a greater share of the hot element, and which a lesser.

beads.greek: καὶ ὡς διὰ τοῦτ’ αὐτὸ τὰ μὲν θερμότερα φύσει, τὰ δὲ ψυχρότερα γέγονεν.
beads.english: And that for this very reason some have come to be hotter by nature, others colder.

beads.greek: ἅπασι γὰρ ἡμῖν ὑπάρχει τὸ θερμὸν στοιχεῖον ἔμφυ τον ἐκ πρώτης ἀρχῆς, ἣν ἐκ σπέρματός τε καὶ καταμηνίου κεκτήμεθα.
beads.english: For in all of us the hot element is present innately from the first beginning, which we possess from the seed and the menstrual blood.

beads.greek: διαφέρομεν δ’ ἀλλήλων ἐν τῷ μᾶλλόν τε καὶ ἧττον εἶναι θερμοί· ἀλλ’ εἰσὶ γέ τινες ὅροι τούτου τοῦ πλάτους, ὧν ἐπέκεινα τῆς κράσεως ἐξικομένης ἤτοι νοσεῖν ἡμῖν ἀναγκαῖόν ἐστιν ἢ διαφθείρεσθαι.
beads.english: We differ from one another in being more or less hot; but there are certain limits to this latitude, and when the mixture goes beyond them it is necessary for us either to fall ill or to perish.

διαφέρομεν δ’ ἀλλήλων ἐν τῷ μᾶλλόν τε καὶ ἧττον εἶναι θερμοί· ἀλλ’ εἰσὶ γέ τινες ὅροι τούτου τοῦ πλάτους, ὧν ἐπέκεινα τῆς κράσεως ἐξικομένης ἤτοι νοσεῖν ἡμῖν ἀναγκαῖόν ἐστιν ἢ διαφθείρεσθαι.
english_sentences: That there is heat in us is evidently apparent to all; but whether this has its origin from the motion in the heart and the arteries, or whether, just as motion itself [199] is innate in the heart, in the same way the heat is too, is a matter of dispute among physicians.

But whoever wishes to learn in a scientific manner that the principles of generation for all animals are the hot, the cold, the dry and the wet has one book written by me, in which I expound and demonstrate the opinion of Hippocrates.
This book is entitled On the Elements according to Hippocrates.
And following it there are others, those On Mixtures, in which I show which bodies have in themselves a greater share of the hot element, and which a lesser.
And that for this very reason some have come to be hotter by nature, others colder.
For in all of us the hot element is present innately from the first beginning, which we possess from the seed and the menstrual blood.
We differ from one another in being more or less hot; but there are certain limits to this latitude, and when the mixture goes beyond them it is necessary for us either to fall ill or to perish.

beads.greek: καὶ γὰρ ἐπὶ πλέον ψυχθέντες ἐν νοσήματι ψυχρῷ καθιστάμεθα [200] καὶ θερμανθέντες ἔξω τοῦ κατὰ τὴν ὑγείαν πλάτους εἰς πυρετὸν ἀγόμεθα.
beads.english: For indeed, when we are cooled to excess we come to be in a cold disease, [200] and when we are heated beyond the latitude that belongs to health we are brought into fever.

beads.greek: καὶ τοίνυν καὶ τῶν πυρετῶν αὐτῶν ἔνιοι μὲν ἀκριβῶς εἰσι ξηροὶ, καθάπερ οἱ ἀκριβῶς καῦσοι, τινὲς δὲ ἐσχάτως ὑγροὶ, καθάπερ οἱ τυφώδεις ὀνομαζόμενοι.
beads.english: And moreover, of the fevers themselves some are precisely dry, like the exact burning fevers (kausoi), while some are extremely wet, like those called typhous (typhodeis).

beads.greek: εἰ δ’ οὐ χαίρει τις τοῖς οὕτω καλουμένοις ἢ κατ’ ἄλλου πράγματος ἐπιφέρειν εἴθισται τὰς εἰρημένας προσηγορίας, ἐγὼ τούτῳ τῷ λόγῳ διηγήσομαι τοὺς ὑγροὺς πυρετοὺς ὁποίους εἶναί φημι.
beads.english: But if someone does not like things so named, or is accustomed to apply the aforesaid appellations to some other thing, I shall explain in this discourse what kind of fevers I say the wet fevers are.

beads.greek: ἱδροῦσι μὲν οἱ κάμνοντες ἀπὸ πρώτης ἡμέρας, ἐν δ’ αὐτοῖς ἱδρῶσιν ἢ μετρίως ἢ οὐδὲν ὀνινάμενοι, τούτους ὑγροὺς ἐγὼ τοὺς πυρετοὺς ὀνομάζω, ξηροὺς δὲ ἔμπαλιν ἐκείνους καλῶ τῶν πυρετῶν, οἷς δίψα σφοδρὰ καὶ γλῶττα ξηρὰ καὶ δέρμα σκληρὸν οἷόν περ βύρσα καὶ πολὺς αὐχμὸς ἐν ἅπαντι τῷ σώματι.
beads.english: The patients sweat from the first day, yet are benefited by these sweats either moderately or not at all: these fevers I call wet; and conversely I call dry those fevers in which there is violent thirst, a dry tongue, skin hard like a hide, and much parching dryness throughout the whole body.

beads.greek: καὶ μὴν καὶ ἕτεροί τινές εἰσι πυρετοὶ τὴν διαπνοὴν ὅλου τοῦ σώματος ἔχοντες ἀνιαρὰν τοῖς ἁπτομένοις, ὡς νύττεσθαί τε καὶ δάκνεσθαι δοκεῖν, διχῶς καὶ τούτου γινομένου, ποτὲ μὲν ἀερώδους ξηροῦ τοῦ προσπίπτοντος ἡμῖν, ἔστι δ’ ὅτε ὑγροῦ πως φαινομένου, καθάπερ ἀτμοῦ τινος.
beads.english: And further there are certain other fevers in which the transpiration of the whole body is distressing to those who touch it, so that they seem to be pricked and bitten; and this too happens in two ways, sometimes what strikes us being dry and airy, and at other times appearing somehow moist, like a kind of vapour.

greek_sentences: καὶ γὰρ ἐπὶ πλέον ψυχθέντες ἐν νοσήματι ψυχρῷ καθιστάμεθα [200] καὶ θερμανθέντες ἔξω τοῦ κατὰ τὴν ὑγείαν πλάτους εἰς πυρετὸν ἀγόμεθα.
καὶ τοίνυν καὶ τῶν πυρετῶν αὐτῶν ἔνιοι μὲν ἀκριβῶς εἰσι ξηροὶ, καθάπερ οἱ ἀκριβῶς καῦσοι, τινὲς δὲ ἐσχάτως ὑγροὶ, καθάπερ οἱ τυφώδεις ὀνομαζόμενοι.
εἰ δ’ οὐ χαίρει τις τοῖς οὕτω καλουμένοις ἢ κατ’ ἄλλου πράγματος ἐπιφέρειν εἴθισται τὰς εἰρημένας προσηγορίας, ἐγὼ τούτῳ τῷ λόγῳ διηγήσομαι τοὺς ὑγροὺς πυρετοὺς ὁποίους εἶναί φημι.

ἱδροῦσι μὲν οἱ κάμνοντες ἀπὸ πρώτης ἡμέρας, ἐν δ’ αὐτοῖς ἱδρῶσιν ἢ μετρίως ἢ οὐδὲν ὀνινάμενοι, τούτους ὑγροὺς ἐγὼ τοὺς πυρετοὺς ὀνομάζω, ξηροὺς δὲ ἔμπαλιν ἐκείνους καλῶ τῶν πυρετῶν, οἷς δίψα σφοδρὰ καὶ γλῶττα ξηρὰ καὶ δέρμα σκληρὸν οἷόν περ βύρσα καὶ πολὺς αὐχμὸς ἐν ἅπαντι τῷ σώματι.

καὶ μὴν καὶ ἕτεροί τινές εἰσι πυρετοὶ τὴν διαπνοὴν ὅλου τοῦ σώματος ἔχοντες ἀνιαρὰν τοῖς ἁπτομένοις, ὡς νύττεσθαί τε καὶ δάκνεσθαι δοκεῖν, διχῶς καὶ τούτου γινομένου, ποτὲ μὲν ἀερώδους ξηροῦ τοῦ προσπίπτοντος ἡμῖν, ἔστι δ’ ὅτε ὑγροῦ πως φαινομένου, καθάπερ ἀτμοῦ τινος.
english_sentences: For indeed, when we are cooled to excess we come to be in a cold disease, [200] and when we are heated beyond the latitude that belongs to health we are brought into fever.
And moreover, of the fevers themselves some are precisely dry, like the exact burning fevers (kausoi), while some are extremely wet, like those called typhous (typhodeis).
But if someone does not like things so named, or is accustomed to apply the aforesaid appellations to some other thing, I shall explain in this discourse what kind of fevers I say the wet fevers are.

The patients sweat from the first day, yet are benefited by these sweats either moderately or not at all: these fevers I call wet; and conversely I call dry those fevers in which there is violent thirst, a dry tongue, skin hard like a hide, and much parching dryness throughout the whole body.

And further there are certain other fevers in which the transpiration of the whole body is distressing to those who touch it, so that they seem to be pricked and bitten; and this too happens in two ways, sometimes what strikes us being dry and airy, and at other times appearing somehow moist, like a kind of vapour.

beads.greek: τοιαύταις ἰδέαις ἀλλήλων διαφέρουσι καὶ ﻿ [201] τῶν ὑγιαινόντων αὐτῶν αἱ κράσεις, ἃς δὴ καὶ δυσκράτους εἶναί φαμεν, ἐπανορθούμεθά τε καθ’ ὅσον οἷόν τε τὴν φυσικὴν δυσκρασίαν αὐτῶν.
beads.english: By such forms the mixtures even [201] of healthy persons themselves differ from one another—those which indeed we also say are ill-mixed—and we correct their natural ill-mixture as far as possible.

beads.greek: ἔστι γὰρ καὶ τοῦτο μόριον οὐ σμικρὸν τῆς ὑγιεινῆς τέχνης.
beads.english: For this too is no small part of the art of hygiene.

beads.greek: ὅσα δὲ εὔκρατα φύσει τῶν σωμάτων ἐστὶν, οὐδὲν τοιοῦτον ἁπτομένοις ἐμφαίνει.
beads.english: But those bodies which are by nature well-mixed display nothing of this sort to those who touch them.

beads.greek: σύμμετρα γὰρ ἀκριβῶς ἐστιν, ὡς μηδὲν ἐνδεῖν αὐτοῖς τὸ θερμὸν, οἷα γέρουσιν ἢ τοῖς ἐψυγμένοις, μήθ’ ὑπερβάλλειν, ὡς τοῖς ἀμετρότερον πονήσασιν ἢ διατρίψασιν ἐπὶ πλεῖον ἐν ἡλίῳ θερινῷ.
beads.english: For they are precisely well-proportioned, so that the heat is in no way deficient in them, as it is in old men or in those who have been chilled, nor excessive, as in those who have exerted themselves immoderately or spent too long in the summer sun.

beads.greek: πολὺ δὲ δὴ μᾶλλον οὐδὲ τὸ δάκνον ἢ ἀνιαρὸν ἡ τούτων ἔχει θερμασία.
beads.english: And much less still does the heat of these have anything biting or distressing about it.

beads.greek: σαφηνείας δὲ ἕνεκα τῶν λεγομένων οὐδὲν ἂν εἴη χεῖρον ἀναμνησθῆναί σε βαλανείων, ἐν οἷς ἓν μέν ἐστι δήπου τὸ τῶν εὐκράτων εἶδος, αἱ δυσκρασίαι δὲ πολλαί.
beads.english: For the sake of clarity in what is being said, it would be no worse for you to recall baths, in which there is surely one kind of the well-mixed, but the ill-mixtures are many.

beads.greek: μία μὲν γὰρ δυσκρασία βαλανείου, ψυχροτέρου τῆς χρείας ὑπάρχοντος, ἑτέρα δὲ εἰ μέχρι τοῦ λυπεῖν ἤδη θερμανθείη, τρίτη δ’ ἄλλη καθ’ ἣν οὔθ’ ὡς ψυχρότερον οὔθ’ ὡς θερμότερον αἰτιώμενοι πλῆρες ἀτμοῦ φαμεν ὑπάρχειν καὶ κατὰ τοῦτο μεμφόμεθα.
beads.english: For one ill-mixture of a bath is when it is colder than is needed; another, if it has been heated to the point of already causing distress; and a third, different one, in which, finding fault with it neither as colder nor as hotter, we say that it is full of vapour and blame it on this account.

greek_sentences: τοιαύταις ἰδέαις ἀλλήλων διαφέρουσι καὶ ﻿ [201] τῶν ὑγιαινόντων αὐτῶν αἱ κράσεις, ἃς δὴ καὶ δυσκράτους εἶναί φαμεν, ἐπανορθούμεθά τε καθ’ ὅσον οἷόν τε τὴν φυσικὴν δυσκρασίαν αὐτῶν.
ἔστι γὰρ καὶ τοῦτο μόριον οὐ σμικρὸν τῆς ὑγιεινῆς τέχνης.
ὅσα δὲ εὔκρατα φύσει τῶν σωμάτων ἐστὶν, οὐδὲν τοιοῦτον ἁπτομένοις ἐμφαίνει.
σύμμετρα γὰρ ἀκριβῶς ἐστιν, ὡς μηδὲν ἐνδεῖν αὐτοῖς τὸ θερμὸν, οἷα γέρουσιν ἢ τοῖς ἐψυγμένοις, μήθ’ ὑπερβάλλειν, ὡς τοῖς ἀμετρότερον πονήσασιν ἢ διατρίψασιν ἐπὶ πλεῖον ἐν ἡλίῳ θερινῷ.
πολὺ δὲ δὴ μᾶλλον οὐδὲ τὸ δάκνον ἢ ἀνιαρὸν ἡ τούτων ἔχει θερμασία.
σαφηνείας δὲ ἕνεκα τῶν λεγομένων οὐδὲν ἂν εἴη χεῖρον ἀναμνησθῆναί σε βαλανείων, ἐν οἷς ἓν μέν ἐστι δήπου τὸ τῶν εὐκράτων εἶδος, αἱ δυσκρασίαι δὲ πολλαί.

μία μὲν γὰρ δυσκρασία βαλανείου, ψυχροτέρου τῆς χρείας ὑπάρχοντος, ἑτέρα δὲ εἰ μέχρι τοῦ λυπεῖν ἤδη θερμανθείη, τρίτη δ’ ἄλλη καθ’ ἣν οὔθ’ ὡς ψυχρότερον οὔθ’ ὡς θερμότερον αἰτιώμενοι πλῆρες ἀτμοῦ φαμεν ὑπάρχειν καὶ κατὰ τοῦτο μεμφόμεθα.
english_sentences: By such forms the mixtures even [201] of healthy persons themselves differ from one another—those which indeed we also say are ill-mixed—and we correct their natural ill-mixture as far as possible.
For this too is no small part of the art of hygiene.
But those bodies which are by nature well-mixed display nothing of this sort to those who touch them.

For they are precisely well-proportioned, so that the heat is in no way deficient in them, as it is in old men or in those who have been chilled, nor excessive, as in those who have exerted themselves immoderately or spent too long in the summer sun.
And much less still does the heat of these have anything biting or distressing about it.
For the sake of clarity in what is being said, it would be no worse for you to recall baths, in which there is surely one kind of the well-mixed, but the ill-mixtures are many.

For one ill-mixture of a bath is when it is colder than is needed; another, if it has been heated to the point of already causing distress; and a third, different one, in which, finding fault with it neither as colder nor as hotter, we say that it is full of vapour and blame it on this account.

beads.greek: τίς γὰρ οὐκ οἶδεν, εἴ γε ὅλως ἄνθρωπός ἐστιν, ὡς εὔκρατόν ἐστι μὲν [202] ὕδωρ πολλάκις, ἔστι δ’ ὁμοίως αὐτῷ ὁ καὶ ἀὴρ καὶ ἀτμός.
beads.english: For who does not know, if he is a human being at all, that water is often well-mixed, [202] and that air and vapour are likewise so along with it?

beads.greek: οὕτω γοῦν καὶ λίθος εὔκρατος ἐν αὐτοῖς τοῖς βαλανείοις γίγνεται, καθ’ οὗ κυλινδεῖσθαι δυνατὸν, οὕτε θερμασίαν ὑπερβάλλουσαν οὔτε ψύξιν αἰτιώμενον, οὔτ’ αὐχμὸν ἢ πλῆθος ὑγρότητος.
beads.english: So at any rate a stone too becomes well-mixed in the baths themselves, one on which it is possible to roll about, finding fault neither with excessive heat nor with cold, nor with dryness or an abundance of moisture.

beads.greek: ὥσπερ οὖν ἐν ὕδατι καὶ λίθῳ καὶ ἀέρι σύμμετρος γίγνεται θερμότης, οὕτως καὶ κατὰ τὸν ἀτμὸν, ὃς ἐπειδὰν εὔκρατος ὢν ἐμπλήσει τὸ βαλανεῖον, οἱ λουόμενοι δυσχεραίνουσι μὲν καὶ μέμφονται τὸ τοιοῦτον λουτρὸν, ψυχρότερον δὲ ἢ θερμότερον οὐκ ὀνομάζουσιν, ὡς εἴ γε καὶ τοιοῦτόν τι ποιεῖ, διττὴν ποιοῦνται τὴν κατηγορίαν τοῦ βαλανείου, ψυχρὸν εἶναι φάσκοντες αὐτὸ καὶ μεστὸν ἀτμοῦ, καθάπερ γε καὶ θερμὸν αὖθις ἀμέτρως σὺν ἀτμῷ δαψι λεῖ.
beads.english: Just as, then, in water, stone and air a well-proportioned heat comes about, so too in the case of vapour, which, when it fills the bath while being well-mixed, the bathers are vexed and find fault with such a bath, yet do not call it colder or hotter; since, if indeed it does produce some such effect as well, they make a twofold accusation against the bath, declaring that it is cold and full of vapour, just as, conversely, that it is immoderately hot together with abundant vapour.

greek_sentences: τίς γὰρ οὐκ οἶδεν, εἴ γε ὅλως ἄνθρωπός ἐστιν, ὡς εὔκρατόν ἐστι μὲν [202] ὕδωρ πολλάκις, ἔστι δ’ ὁμοίως αὐτῷ ὁ καὶ ἀὴρ καὶ ἀτμός.
οὕτω γοῦν καὶ λίθος εὔκρατος ἐν αὐτοῖς τοῖς βαλανείοις γίγνεται, καθ’ οὗ κυλινδεῖσθαι δυνατὸν, οὕτε θερμασίαν ὑπερβάλλουσαν οὔτε ψύξιν αἰτιώμενον, οὔτ’ αὐχμὸν ἢ πλῆθος ὑγρότητος.

ὥσπερ οὖν ἐν ὕδατι καὶ λίθῳ καὶ ἀέρι σύμμετρος γίγνεται θερμότης, οὕτως καὶ κατὰ τὸν ἀτμὸν, ὃς ἐπειδὰν εὔκρατος ὢν ἐμπλήσει τὸ βαλανεῖον, οἱ λουόμενοι δυσχεραίνουσι μὲν καὶ μέμφονται τὸ τοιοῦτον λουτρὸν, ψυχρότερον δὲ ἢ θερμότερον οὐκ ὀνομάζουσιν, ὡς εἴ γε καὶ τοιοῦτόν τι ποιεῖ, διττὴν ποιοῦνται τὴν κατηγορίαν τοῦ βαλανείου, ψυχρὸν εἶναι φάσκοντες αὐτὸ καὶ μεστὸν ἀτμοῦ, καθάπερ γε καὶ θερμὸν αὖθις ἀμέτρως σὺν ἀτμῷ δαψι λεῖ.

So at any rate a stone too becomes well-mixed in the baths themselves, one on which it is possible to roll about, finding fault neither with excessive heat nor with cold, nor with dryness or an abundance of moisture.

beads.greek: μὴ τοίνυν ἐπιλανθανώμεθα τούτων μηδὲ τὰ κοινῇ πᾶσιν ἀνθρώποις γιγνωσκόμενα διαφθείρωμεν ὑπὸ περιττῆς σοφίας, ἣν ἐπιδείκνυνταί τινες, ἀλλὰ μεμνημένοι τῶν βαλανείων, ἐπειδὰν ἀκούσωμέν τινος ἐπὶ ζώου λέγοντος, ὡς ἔστι τούτου μὲν εὔκρατον τὸ θερμὸν, τούτου δὲ δύσκρατον, [203] οὐκ ἐπ’ ἄλλο τι μεταφέρωμεν τὴν διάνοιαν, ἀλλ’ ἐφ’ ὅπερ ἅπαντες οἱ τὰς κοινὰς ἐννοίας διασώζοντες ἄνθρωποι, καθ’ ἑκάστην ἡμέραν ἐν ἄλλοις τε πολλοῖς καὶ μέντοι γε καὶ τοῖς βαλανείοις ὧν ἐμνημόνευσα.
beads.english: Let us not, then, forget these things, nor corrupt what is known in common to all men through the superfluous wisdom which some people display; but, bearing the baths in mind, whenever we hear someone saying of an animal that the heat of this one is well-mixed, while that of this other is ill-mixed, [203] let us not transfer our thought to anything else, but to that very thing to which all men who preserve the common notions transfer it every day, in many other matters and indeed also in the baths which I have mentioned.

beads.greek: θερμὸν γοῦν εἷναί φασι τὸ βαλανεῖον καὶ ψυχρὸν, εἶτ’ αὖθις ἀτμοῦ πλῆρες ἢ ξηρὸν καὶ αὐχμῶδες καὶ ἑκάστῳ τῶν ὀνομάτων ἴδιόν τι δηλοῦντες πρᾶγμα.
beads.english: They say, at any rate, that the bath is hot or cold, and then again full of vapour or dry and parched, indicating by each of the names some particular thing.

beads.greek: πρὸς τοίνυν τοῖς εἰρημένοις ἕτερόν τι βαλανεῖόν ἐστι καπνοῦ πλῆρες καὶ ναὶ μὰ Δία γε τούτου πολυειδεστάτου.
beads.english: In addition, then, to those mentioned, there is another sort of bath, full of smoke—and, yes by Zeus, of smoke of the most varied kinds.

beads.greek: ἕτερος μὲν ὁ ἐκ δρυίνων ξύλων, ἕτερος δὲ ὁ ἐκ συκίνων ἢ ἐλαΐνων ἐστὶ καὶ καθ’ ἕκαστόν γε δένδρον ἄλλος καὶ ἄλλος.
beads.english: One is that from oak wood, another that from fig or olive wood, and for each tree there is a different one.

beads.greek: ἀλλ’ οὐδέπω δέομαι τῶν κατὰ μέρος διαφορῶν.
beads.english: But I do not yet need the particular differences.

beads.greek: ἀρκεῖ γάρ μοι τήν γε πρώτην ὅλον γε τὸ γένος τοῦτο μιᾷ κλήσει καὶ νοήσει περιλαμβάνοντι καπνώδη τὸν ἀέρα φάναι τοῦ βαλανείου, μηδ’ ἐνταῦθα μεμφόμενον αὐτοῦ θερμασίαν ἢ ψύξιν ἢ ὥσπερ γε μεμφόμενον αὖθις, εἰ οὕτως ἔτυχε κατ’ ἄμφω, καὶ ὡς θερμὸν τὸ βαλανεῖον καὶ ὡς καπνῶδες.
beads.english: For it suffices me, for the present at least, embracing this whole genus under a single name and notion, to say that the air of the bath is smoky, here too not finding fault with its heat or coldness—or, as the case may be, finding fault with it again on both counts, if it so happens, both as hot and as smoky.

θερμὸν γοῦν εἷναί φασι τὸ βαλανεῖον καὶ ψυχρὸν, εἶτ’ αὖθις ἀτμοῦ πλῆρες ἢ ξηρὸν καὶ αὐχμῶδες καὶ ἑκάστῳ τῶν ὀνομάτων ἴδιόν τι δηλοῦντες πρᾶγμα.

ἀλλ’ οὐδέπω δέομαι τῶν κατὰ μέρος διαφορῶν.

ἀρκεῖ γάρ μοι τήν γε πρώτην ὅλον γε τὸ γένος τοῦτο μιᾷ κλήσει καὶ νοήσει περιλαμβάνοντι καπνώδη τὸν ἀέρα φάναι τοῦ βαλανείου, μηδ’ ἐνταῦθα μεμφόμενον αὐτοῦ θερμασίαν ἢ ψύξιν ἢ ὥσπερ γε μεμφόμενον αὖθις, εἰ οὕτως ἔτυχε κατ’ ἄμφω, καὶ ὡς θερμὸν τὸ βαλανεῖον καὶ ὡς καπνῶδες.
english_sentences: Let us not, then, forget these things, nor corrupt what is known in common to all men through the superfluous wisdom which some people display; but, bearing the baths in mind, whenever we hear someone saying of an animal that the heat of this one is well-mixed, while that of this other is ill-mixed, [203] let us not transfer our thought to anything else, but to that very thing to which all men who preserve the common notions transfer it every day, in many other matters and indeed also in the baths which I have mentioned.
They say, at any rate, that the bath is hot or cold, and then again full of vapour or dry and parched, indicating by each of the names some particular thing.
In addition, then, to those mentioned, there is another sort of bath, full of smoke—and, yes by Zeus, of smoke of the most varied kinds.
One is that from oak wood, another that from fig or olive wood, and for each tree there is a different one.
But I do not yet need the particular differences.

For it suffices me, for the present at least, embracing this whole genus under a single name and notion, to say that the air of the bath is smoky, here too not finding fault with its heat or coldness—or, as the case may be, finding fault with it again on both counts, if it so happens, both as hot and as smoky.

beads.greek: ἐάσης οὖν ἤδη τὰ βαλανεῖα τῶν καθ’ ἑκάστην [204] ἡμέραν ἐν ταῖς οἰκίαις ἡμῖν συμβαινόντων ἀναμνήσθητί μοι, ποτὲ μὲν ὑγρότητα τῶν οἰκίων ἐν οἷς ἔσμεν, ἔστι δ’ ὅτε ἄμετρον ψύξιν ἢ θερμότητα μεμφόμεθα, πότερα μὲν οὖν ὁμοίως μεμφόμεθα τὸν κατὰ τὸν οἶκον ἀέρα τοῖς ὑπὸ κύνα καύμασι, κἀπειδὰν καπνοῦ πληρωθῇ, ἢ κἀνταῦθα ὥσπερ ἐν ταῖς βαλανείοις ἔστιν ὅτε κατὰ μὲν τὴν θερμασίαν διαλλάττουσιν οὐδὲν, ἔστι δ’ αὐτῶν ὁ μὲν αὐτὸ δὴ τοῦτο μόνον, ἀὴρ θερμὸς, ὁ δὲ σὺν τούτῳ καπνώδης, εἶτα ὁ μέν γε θερμὸς ἀὴρ οὐδέποτε προκαλεῖται δάκρυον, τῷ καπνώδει δ’ ἀεὶ ὑπάρχει τοῦτο κἂν μετρίως θερμὸς ᾖ, ὥστε ἐναργῶς ἐνταῦθα κατάδηλόν ἐστι τὸ δακνῶδες θερμὸν οὐ τῷ μᾶλλον θερμαίνειν, ἀλλ’ ἑτέρῳ τινὶ διαλλάττον.
beads.english: Leaving the baths now, then, recall for me what happens to us every [204] day in our houses: sometimes we find fault with the dampness of the houses in which we are, at other times with immoderate cold or heat. Do we then find fault with the air in the house in the same way in the heats under the Dog-star as when it has been filled with smoke, or is it here too, as in the baths, that sometimes they differ not at all in heat, yet one of them is just this alone, hot air, while the other is, along with this, smoky; and then the hot air never provokes tears, whereas the smoky air always does this, even if it is only moderately hot; so that here it is evidently plain that the biting heat differs not by heating more, but by something else.

beads.greek: ἐγγυτάτῳ γοῦν φλογὸς μεγίστης ἀκάπνου στάντες θερμαινόμεθα οὕτω πολλάκις, ὡς ἐγγὺς μὲν ἥκειν τοῦ καίεσθαι, δάκνεται δ’ οὐδεὶς οὐδὲ δακρύει τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς ὡς ἀπὸ καπνοῦ.
beads.english: At any rate, standing very close to a very great smokeless flame we are often heated to such a degree as to come near to being burned, yet no one is bitten, nor do his eyes water as from smoke.

greek_sentences: ἐάσης οὖν ἤδη τὰ βαλανεῖα τῶν καθ’ ἑκάστην [204] ἡμέραν ἐν ταῖς οἰκίαις ἡμῖν συμβαινόντων ἀναμνήσθητί μοι, ποτὲ μὲν ὑγρότητα τῶν οἰκίων ἐν οἷς ἔσμεν, ἔστι δ’ ὅτε ἄμετρον ψύξιν ἢ θερμότητα μεμφόμεθα, πότερα μὲν οὖν ὁμοίως μεμφόμεθα τὸν κατὰ τὸν οἶκον ἀέρα τοῖς ὑπὸ κύνα καύμασι, κἀπειδὰν καπνοῦ πληρωθῇ, ἢ κἀνταῦθα ὥσπερ ἐν ταῖς βαλανείοις ἔστιν ὅτε κατὰ μὲν τὴν θερμασίαν διαλλάττουσιν οὐδὲν, ἔστι δ’ αὐτῶν ὁ μὲν αὐτὸ δὴ τοῦτο μόνον, ἀὴρ θερμὸς, ὁ δὲ σὺν τούτῳ καπνώδης, εἶτα ὁ μέν γε θερμὸς ἀὴρ οὐδέποτε προκαλεῖται δάκρυον, τῷ καπνώδει δ’ ἀεὶ ὑπάρχει τοῦτο κἂν μετρίως θερμὸς ᾖ, ὥστε ἐναργῶς ἐνταῦθα κατάδηλόν ἐστι τὸ δακνῶδες θερμὸν οὐ τῷ μᾶλλον θερμαίνειν, ἀλλ’ ἑτέρῳ τινὶ διαλλάττον.
ἐγγυτάτῳ γοῦν φλογὸς μεγίστης ἀκάπνου στάντες θερμαινόμεθα οὕτω πολλάκις, ὡς ἐγγὺς μὲν ἥκειν τοῦ καίεσθαι, δάκνεται δ’ οὐδεὶς οὐδὲ δακρύει τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς ὡς ἀπὸ καπνοῦ.
english_sentences: Leaving the baths now, then, recall for me what happens to us every [204] day in our houses: sometimes we find fault with the dampness of the houses in which we are, at other times with immoderate cold or heat.

Do we then find fault with the air in the house in the same way in the heats under the Dog-star as when it has been filled with smoke, or is it here too, as in the baths, that sometimes they differ not at all in heat, yet one of them is just this alone, hot air, while the other is, along with this, smoky; and then the hot air never provokes tears, whereas the smoky air always does this, even if it is only moderately hot; so that here it is evidently plain that the biting heat differs not by heating more, but by something else.
At any rate, standing very close to a very great smokeless flame we are often heated to such a degree as to come near to being burned, yet no one is bitten, nor do his eyes water as from smoke.

beads.greek: θαυμαστὸν οὖν εἴ τις ἐπὶ καπνοῦ καὶ φλογὸς αἰσθάνεται [205] τῆς διαφορᾶς, ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν ἡμετέρων σωμάτων ἀναίσθητός ἐστιν ἐνίοτε μὲν ἰσχυροτάτης θερμασίας οἷον φλογὸς, ἐνίοτε δὲ ἀνιαρᾶς καὶ δακνώδους οἷόν περ καπνοῦ.
beads.english: It is astonishing, then, if someone perceives [205] the difference in the case of smoke and flame, but in the case of our bodies is insensible of a heat that is sometimes very strong, like that of flame, and sometimes distressing and biting, like that of smoke.

beads.greek: θαυμάζω δὲ οὐδὲν ἧττον, εἰ μὴ συγχωρεῖ τὰς κατὰ τὸ θερμὸν ἐν τοῖς ζώοις δυσκρασίας ἀνάλογον ἔχειν ταῖς κατὰ τὰ βαλανεῖα καὶ τὰς οἰκίας· ὡς οὖν ἐν ταῖς οἰκίαις ἄλλος μὲν ἀήρ ἐστιν οἴκου καπνώδους, ἄλλος δὲ ἁπλῶς θερμοῦ, κατὰ τὸν αὐτὸν οἶμαι τρόπον ἕτερος τούτων ἐναργῶς ἐστὶν ἐν ᾧ πλῆθός ἐστι καιομένων λύχνων ἢ δᾳδὸς ἅμα λιγνύσι, καὶ τοίνυν καὶ καλοῦμεν, ὥσπερ τὸν ἕτερον ἀέρα καπνώδη, λιγνυώδη τοῦτο, ἐξ ὑπεροπτήσεως ὕλης γενόμενον.
beads.english: And I am no less astonished if he does not concede that the ill-mixtures in respect of heat in animals are analogous to those in baths and houses; as, then, in houses the air of a smoky house is one thing, and that of a simply hot house another, in the same way, I think, evidently different from these is that air in which there is a multitude of burning lamps or of torch-wood together with soot, and accordingly we also call this sooty, just as we call the other air smoky, since it arises from the over-roasting of material.

beads.greek: ἡ γάρ τοι λιγνὺς ταύτῃ τοῦ καπνοῦ διενήνοχε, καίτοι γε ἀμφοῖν περιττωμάτων ὑπαρχόντων φλογὸς, ὅτι ἡ λιγνύς ἐστι μὲν κατωπτημένης ὕλης γεώδης ἀναθυμίασις, καπνὸς δὲ οὔθ’ ὑπερωπτημένης οὔτε γεώδης, ἀλλ’ ἡμικαύστου τε καὶ συμμιγοῦς ἔξ ὑγρᾶς καὶ γεώδους οὐσίας.
beads.english: For soot differs from smoke in this respect—although both are residues of flame—that soot is an earthy exhalation of material that has been roasted through, whereas smoke is neither of over-roasted material nor earthy, but of material that is half-burnt and mixed from a moist and an earthy substance.

greek_sentences: θαυμαστὸν οὖν εἴ τις ἐπὶ καπνοῦ καὶ φλογὸς αἰσθάνεται [205] τῆς διαφορᾶς, ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν ἡμετέρων σωμάτων ἀναίσθητός ἐστιν ἐνίοτε μὲν ἰσχυροτάτης θερμασίας οἷον φλογὸς, ἐνίοτε δὲ ἀνιαρᾶς καὶ δακνώδους οἷόν περ καπνοῦ.

ἡ γάρ τοι λιγνὺς ταύτῃ τοῦ καπνοῦ διενήνοχε, καίτοι γε ἀμφοῖν περιττωμάτων ὑπαρχόντων φλογὸς, ὅτι ἡ λιγνύς ἐστι μὲν κατωπτημένης ὕλης γεώδης ἀναθυμίασις, καπνὸς δὲ οὔθ’ ὑπερωπτημένης οὔτε γεώδης, ἀλλ’ ἡμικαύστου τε καὶ συμμιγοῦς ἔξ ὑγρᾶς καὶ γεώδους οὐσίας.
english_sentences: It is astonishing, then, if someone perceives [205] the difference in the case of smoke and flame, but in the case of our bodies is insensible of a heat that is sometimes very strong, like that of flame, and sometimes distressing and biting, like that of smoke.

And I am no less astonished if he does not concede that the ill-mixtures in respect of heat in animals are analogous to those in baths and houses; as, then, in houses the air of a smoky house is one thing, and that of a simply hot house another, in the same way, I think, evidently different from these is that air in which there is a multitude of burning lamps or of torch-wood together with soot, and accordingly we also call this sooty, just as we call the other air smoky, since it arises from the over-roasting of material.

For soot differs from smoke in this respect—although both are residues of flame—that soot is an earthy exhalation of material that has been roasted through, whereas smoke is neither of over-roasted material nor earthy, but of material that is half-burnt and mixed from a moist and an earthy substance.

beads.greek: ὅστις οὖν ἐπαιδεύθη νομίμως ἐν Ἱπποκρατείοις δόγμασιν, ἔμαθεν οὗτος ὡς τῆς ὀνομαζομένης ἤδη συνήθως ἅπασι τοῖς ἰατροῖς ἀδήλου ﻿ [206] διαπνοῆς, ἣν διαπνεῖται τὰ σώματα, τὸ μὲν τοιοῦτόν ἐστιν οἷον ἀτμὸς, ἕτερον δὲ οἷον ἀὴρ ξηρὸς, ἕτερον δὲ σὺν αἰσθηταῖς ὑγρότησιν ἐκπῖπτον.
beads.english: Whoever, then, has been properly educated in the Hippocratic doctrines has learned that, of what is by now customarily named by all physicians the insensible [206] transpiration, by which bodies transpire, one kind is such as vapour, another such as dry air, and another falls out together with perceptible moistures.

beads.greek: λείπει τινά.
beads.english: Something is missing.

beads.greek: Αὕτη μὲν ἡ ῥῆσίς ἐστι τῶν ὑπὸ τοῦ Λύκου γεγραμμένων εἰς κατασκευὴν τοῦ μηδὲν διαφέρειν ἕτερον ἑτέρου θερμὸν οὐκ ἀναμένουσα τὸν ἔξωθεν ἔλεγχον, ἀλλ’ ἑαυτὴν καταβάλλουσα. τί γάρ δὴ καί φησι;
beads.english: This, then, is the passage from what Lycus has written toward establishing that one hot thing differs in nothing from another, a passage that does not wait for refutation from outside but overthrows itself.

beads.greek: τὸ θερμὸν ᾗ νενόηται θερμὸν, οὐδεμίαν ἔχει παραλλαγὴν πρὸς ἕτερον θερμόν. εἰ μὲν οὖν οὐδὲν ἐν τῷ λόγῳ σημαίνει τὸ ᾗ νενόηται θερμὸν, ἐξαιρείσθω τελέως αὐτοῦ.
beads.english: For what in fact does he say? ‘The hot, insofar as it is conceived as hot, has no variation with respect to another hot.’ If, then, the phrase ‘insofar as it is conceived as hot’ signifies nothing in the argument, let it be removed from it entirely.

beads.greek: σημαίνων δ’ ἔτι σαφῶς ἐνδείκνυται ταύτῃ μὲν μὴ διαφέρειν τὸ θερμὸν τοῦ θερμοῦ, καθ’ ἕτερον δέ τι διαφέρειν.
beads.english: But if it does signify something, it still clearly indicates that in this respect the hot does not differ from the hot, but that in some other respect it does differ.

greek_sentences: ὅστις οὖν ἐπαιδεύθη νομίμως ἐν Ἱπποκρατείοις δόγμασιν, ἔμαθεν οὗτος ὡς τῆς ὀνομαζομένης ἤδη συνήθως ἅπασι τοῖς ἰατροῖς ἀδήλου ﻿ [206] διαπνοῆς, ἣν διαπνεῖται τὰ σώματα, τὸ μὲν τοιοῦτόν ἐστιν οἷον ἀτμὸς, ἕτερον δὲ οἷον ἀὴρ ξηρὸς, ἕτερον δὲ σὺν αἰσθηταῖς ὑγρότησιν ἐκπῖπτον.
λείπει τινά.

τί γάρ δὴ καί φησι;
τὸ θερμὸν ᾗ νενόηται θερμὸν, οὐδεμίαν ἔχει παραλλαγὴν πρὸς ἕτερον θερμόν.
εἰ μὲν οὖν οὐδὲν ἐν τῷ λόγῳ σημαίνει τὸ ᾗ νενόηται θερμὸν, ἐξαιρείσθω τελέως αὐτοῦ.
σημαίνων δ’ ἔτι σαφῶς ἐνδείκνυται ταύτῃ μὲν μὴ διαφέρειν τὸ θερμὸν τοῦ θερμοῦ, καθ’ ἕτερον δέ τι διαφέρειν.
english_sentences: Whoever, then, has been properly educated in the Hippocratic doctrines has learned that, of what is by now customarily named by all physicians the insensible [206] transpiration, by which bodies transpire, one kind is such as vapour, another such as dry air, and another falls out together with perceptible moistures.
Something is missing.

This, then, is the passage from what Lycus has written toward establishing that one hot thing differs in nothing from another, a passage that does not wait for refutation from outside but overthrows itself.

For what in fact does he say? ‘The hot, insofar as it is conceived as hot, has no variation with respect to another hot.’ If, then, the phrase ‘insofar as it is conceived as hot’ signifies nothing in the argument, let it be removed from it entirely.
But if it does signify something, it still clearly indicates that in this respect the hot does not differ from the hot, but that in some other respect it does differ.

beads.greek: εἰ μὲν γὰρ οὐδαμῇ διαφέρει, περιττῶς πρόσκειται τὸ ᾗ· εἰ δὲ ἄλλῃ μέν πη διαφέρει, ταύτῃ δ’ οὐ διαφέρει, καθ’ ὃ διαφέρει, κατὰ τοῦτο [207] νοείσθωσαν αἱ διαφοραὶ.
beads.english: For if it differs in no way at all, the ‘insofar as’ is added superfluously; but if it differs in some other respect, while in this respect it does not differ, then let the differences be conceived in that respect [207] in which it differs.

beads.greek: ὡς εἴ γε. καθ’ ὃ λέγεται μόνον ἕκαστον σκοποῖτο, πάντων τῶν πραγμάτων ἀναιρήσεις τὰς διαφοράς.
beads.english: Since if one were to consider each thing only in the respect in which it is spoken of, you will abolish the differences of all things.

beads.greek: τὸ ζῶον ᾗ νενόηται ζῶον οὐδὲν ἑτέρου διαφέρει ζώου.
beads.english: The animal, insofar as it is conceived as animal, differs in nothing from another animal.

beads.greek: τὸ φυτὸν ᾗ νενόηται φυτὸν, οὐδὲν ἑτέρου διαφέρει φυτοῦ.
beads.english: The plant, insofar as it is conceived as plant, differs in nothing from another plant.

beads.greek: τὸ δένδρον ᾗ νενόηται δένδρον, οὐδὲν ἑτέρου διαφέρει δένδρου.
beads.english: The tree, insofar as it is conceived as tree, differs in nothing from another tree.

beads.greek: ἆρ’ οὐκ εἰσὶ τοῦ ζώου διαφοραὶ, τὸ πτηνὸν καὶ πεζὸν καὶ νηκτὸν καὶ τὸ ἔνυδρον καὶ ἐγγεῖον καὶ ἀέριον ἢ τὸ θνητὸν καὶ ἀθάνατον ἢ τὸ λογικὸν καὶ ἄλογον ἢ τὸ ἥμερον καὶ τὸ ἄγριον ἢ τὸ δειλὸν καὶ ἄλκιμον ἢ τῶν ἄλλων ὧν ἴσμεν ἕκαστον.
beads.english: Are there then no differences of animal: the winged and the footed and the swimming, and the aquatic and the land-dwelling and the aerial, or the mortal and the immortal, or the rational and the irrational, or the tame and the wild, or the cowardly and the brave, or each of the others that we know?

beads.greek: τί γὰρ δεῖ μακρολογεῖν;
beads.english: For why speak at length?

beads.greek: οὕτω τῶν φυτῶν τὸ μὲν δένδρον, τὸ δὲ θάμνος, τὸ δὲ ἄκανθα, τὸ δὲ πόα, τὸ δὲ φρύγανον, ἢ τῶν πάντων, καθ’ ὃ νενόηται ζῶα μηδεμίαν ἐχόντων διαφορὰν, ὅμως καὶ ταύτας ἁπάσας ἃς εἴρηκε καὶ πρὸς ταύτας ἑτέρας οὐκ ὀλίγας ἀληθῶς ἄν τις εἴποι ζώου διαφοράς;
beads.english: So too among plants one is a tree, another a shrub, another a thorn, another a herb, another brushwood; or, although all of them, in the respect in which they are conceived as animals, have no difference, would one not nonetheless truly call all these which he has mentioned, and not a few others besides these, differences of animal?

beads.greek: οὕτως δὲ κἀπὶ τῶν φυτῶν.
beads.english: And so too in the case of plants.

greek_sentences: εἰ μὲν γὰρ οὐδαμῇ διαφέρει, περιττῶς πρόσκειται τὸ ᾗ· εἰ δὲ ἄλλῃ μέν πη διαφέρει, ταύτῃ δ’ οὐ διαφέρει, καθ’ ὃ διαφέρει, κατὰ τοῦτο [207] νοείσθωσαν αἱ διαφοραὶ.
ὡς εἴ γε.
καθ’ ὃ λέγεται μόνον ἕκαστον σκοποῖτο, πάντων τῶν πραγμάτων ἀναιρήσεις τὰς διαφοράς.
τὸ ζῶον ᾗ νενόηται ζῶον οὐδὲν ἑτέρου διαφέρει ζώου.
τὸ φυτὸν ᾗ νενόηται φυτὸν, οὐδὲν ἑτέρου διαφέρει φυτοῦ.
τὸ δένδρον ᾗ νενόηται δένδρον, οὐδὲν ἑτέρου διαφέρει δένδρου.

ἆρ’ οὐκ εἰσὶ τοῦ ζώου διαφοραὶ, τὸ πτηνὸν καὶ πεζὸν καὶ νηκτὸν καὶ τὸ ἔνυδρον καὶ ἐγγεῖον καὶ ἀέριον ἢ τὸ θνητὸν καὶ ἀθάνατον ἢ τὸ λογικὸν καὶ ἄλογον ἢ τὸ ἥμερον καὶ τὸ ἄγριον ἢ τὸ δειλὸν καὶ ἄλκιμον ἢ τῶν ἄλλων ὧν ἴσμεν ἕκαστον.
τί γὰρ δεῖ μακρολογεῖν;

οὕτω τῶν φυτῶν τὸ μὲν δένδρον, τὸ δὲ θάμνος, τὸ δὲ ἄκανθα, τὸ δὲ πόα, τὸ δὲ φρύγανον, ἢ τῶν πάντων, καθ’ ὃ νενόηται ζῶα μηδεμίαν ἐχόντων διαφορὰν, ὅμως καὶ ταύτας ἁπάσας ἃς εἴρηκε καὶ πρὸς ταύτας ἑτέρας οὐκ ὀλίγας ἀληθῶς ἄν τις εἴποι ζώου διαφοράς;
οὕτως δὲ κἀπὶ τῶν φυτῶν.
english_sentences: For if it differs in no way at all, the ‘insofar as’ is added superfluously; but if it differs in some other respect, while in this respect it does not differ, then let the differences be conceived in that respect [207] in which it differs.
Since if one were to consider each thing only in the respect in which it is spoken of, you will abolish the differences of all things.
The animal, insofar as it is conceived as animal, differs in nothing from another animal.
The plant, insofar as it is conceived as plant, differs in nothing from another plant.
The tree, insofar as it is conceived as tree, differs in nothing from another tree.

Are there then no differences of animal: the winged and the footed and the swimming, and the aquatic and the land-dwelling and the aerial, or the mortal and the immortal, or the rational and the irrational, or the tame and the wild, or the cowardly and the brave, or each of the others that we know?
For why speak at length?

So too among plants one is a tree, another a shrub, another a thorn, another a herb, another brushwood; or, although all of them, in the respect in which they are conceived as animals, have no difference, would one not nonetheless truly call all these which he has mentioned, and not a few others besides these, differences of animal?
And so too in the case of plants.

beads.greek: οὐ γὰρ φυτόν γε φυτοῦ διενήνοχε τῷ τὸ μὲν εἶναι λογικὸν αὐτῶν [208] τὸ δὲ ἄλογον, οὔτε τὸ πτηνὸν ἢ πεζὸν, οὐδὲ τῶν ἄλλων τῶν εἰρημένων οὐδεμία διαφορά.
beads.english: For a plant does not differ from a plant by one of them being rational [208] and the other irrational, nor by the winged or the footed, nor by any of the other differences mentioned.

beads.greek: καθάπερ οὐδὲ ζῶον ζώου διαφέρει τῷ τὸ μὲν εἶναι θάμνος, τὸ δὲ ἄκανθα, τὸ δὲ δένδρον, τὸ δὲ πόα, τὸ δὲ φρύγανον, τὸ δὲ κέδρος, ἀλλ’ ἐν τῷ γένει τῶν φυτῶν ἡ τοιαύτη τομή.
beads.english: Just as neither does an animal differ from an animal by one being a shrub, another a thorn, another a tree, another a herb, another brushwood, another a cedar; rather, such a division belongs within the genus of plants.

beads.greek: ἀλλὰ καὶ νοσημάτων διαφορὰς αὐτὸς ὁ Λύκος γράφει παμπόλλας, καίτοι γε οὐδὲν διαφέρει νόσημα νοσήματος ᾗ νόσημά ἐστιν, ὥσπερ οὐδὲ σύμπτωμα συμπτώματος ᾗ σύμπτωμά ἐστιν, ἀλλ’ ὅμως καὶ τὰς τούτων διαφορὰς ὁ Λύκος ἐπιχειρεῖ γράφειν, ὥσπερ γε καὶ τὰς τῆς πλευρίτιδος, ἑκάστου τε τῶν ἄλλων νοσημάτων.
beads.english: But Lycus himself also writes down a great many differences of diseases, although a disease differs in nothing from a disease insofar as it is a disease, just as neither does a symptom from a symptom insofar as it is a symptom; and yet Lycus undertakes to write down the differences of these too, as indeed also those of pleurisy and of each of the other diseases.

beads.greek: καίτοι γε πλευρῖτις πλευρίτιδος ᾗ πλευρῖτίς ἐστιν οὐδὲν διαφέρει, ἀλλ’ ὅμως ἡ μέν τις εἰς τὴν κλεῖν ἔχει περαινομένην τὴν ὀδύνην, ἡ δ’ εἰς τὸ ὑποχόνδριον.
beads.english: And yet pleurisy differs in nothing from pleurisy insofar as it is pleurisy; but nonetheless one kind has its pain terminating at the collar-bone, another at the hypochondrium.

beads.greek: οὕτω δὲ καὶ μετὰ μὲν τοῦ κεχρῶσθαι τὸ πτύελον ἡ ἑτέρα τῶν πλευριτίδων, ἑτέρα δ’ ἐναντία τῇδε καλουμένη πρὸς ἐνίων ἄπτυστος, ἄλλαι τε πολλαὶ διαφοραὶ, καθ’ ἃς ὑπαλλάττεσθαι συμβαίνει καὶ τὴν θεραπείαν.
beads.english: So too one of the pleurisies goes with the sputum being coloured, while another, opposite to this one, is called by some ‘without sputum’; and there are many other differences, according to which it comes about that the treatment too is varied.

greek_sentences: οὐ γὰρ φυτόν γε φυτοῦ διενήνοχε τῷ τὸ μὲν εἶναι λογικὸν αὐτῶν [208] τὸ δὲ ἄλογον, οὔτε τὸ πτηνὸν ἢ πεζὸν, οὐδὲ τῶν ἄλλων τῶν εἰρημένων οὐδεμία διαφορά.
καθάπερ οὐδὲ ζῶον ζώου διαφέρει τῷ τὸ μὲν εἶναι θάμνος, τὸ δὲ ἄκανθα, τὸ δὲ δένδρον, τὸ δὲ πόα, τὸ δὲ φρύγανον, τὸ δὲ κέδρος, ἀλλ’ ἐν τῷ γένει τῶν φυτῶν ἡ τοιαύτη τομή.

ἀλλὰ καὶ νοσημάτων διαφορὰς αὐτὸς ὁ Λύκος γράφει παμπόλλας, καίτοι γε οὐδὲν διαφέρει νόσημα νοσήματος ᾗ νόσημά ἐστιν, ὥσπερ οὐδὲ σύμπτωμα συμπτώματος ᾗ σύμπτωμά ἐστιν, ἀλλ’ ὅμως καὶ τὰς τούτων διαφορὰς ὁ Λύκος ἐπιχειρεῖ γράφειν, ὥσπερ γε καὶ τὰς τῆς πλευρίτιδος, ἑκάστου τε τῶν ἄλλων νοσημάτων.
καίτοι γε πλευρῖτις πλευρίτιδος ᾗ πλευρῖτίς ἐστιν οὐδὲν διαφέρει, ἀλλ’ ὅμως ἡ μέν τις εἰς τὴν κλεῖν ἔχει περαινομένην τὴν ὀδύνην, ἡ δ’ εἰς τὸ ὑποχόνδριον.

οὕτω δὲ καὶ μετὰ μὲν τοῦ κεχρῶσθαι τὸ πτύελον ἡ ἑτέρα τῶν πλευριτίδων, ἑτέρα δ’ ἐναντία τῇδε καλουμένη πρὸς ἐνίων ἄπτυστος, ἄλλαι τε πολλαὶ διαφοραὶ, καθ’ ἃς ὑπαλλάττεσθαι συμβαίνει καὶ τὴν θεραπείαν.
english_sentences: For a plant does not differ from a plant by one of them being rational [208] and the other irrational, nor by the winged or the footed, nor by any of the other differences mentioned.

Just as neither does an animal differ from an animal by one being a shrub, another a thorn, another a tree, another a herb, another brushwood, another a cedar; rather, such a division belongs within the genus of plants.

But Lycus himself also writes down a great many differences of diseases, although a disease differs in nothing from a disease insofar as it is a disease, just as neither does a symptom from a symptom insofar as it is a symptom; and yet Lycus undertakes to write down the differences of these too, as indeed also those of pleurisy and of each of the other diseases.
And yet pleurisy differs in nothing from pleurisy insofar as it is pleurisy; but nonetheless one kind has its pain terminating at the collar-bone, another at the hypochondrium.

So too one of the pleurisies goes with the sputum being coloured, while another, opposite to this one, is called by some ‘without sputum’; and there are many other differences, according to which it comes about that the treatment too is varied.

beads.greek: ἀλλὰ ἐὰν καὶ [209] ταύτας τῶν πυρετῶν αὐτῶν τὰς διαφορὰς ὁ Λύκος ἐκδιδάσκειν πειρᾶται.
beads.english: But it is so even if [209] Lycus attempts to teach these differences of the fevers themselves.

beads.greek: καίτοι εἴτε κατὰ πλεονεξίαν θερμασίας ἡ γένεσις αὐτοῖς ἐστιν, εἴτε κατὰ τὸ δακνῶδες τῆς ποιότητος, οὐδεμία γενήσεται διαφορὰ πυρετοῦ πρὸς πυρετὸν ᾗ πυρετός ἐστιν.
beads.english: And yet whether their generation is by an excess of heat or by the biting character of the quality, there will be no difference of fever from fever insofar as it is fever.

beads.greek: οὕτως οὖν ἀπαίδευτον ἐρωτᾷ λόγον ὁ Λύκος, ὥστε οὐκ αἰσθάνεται τὰς τέχνας ἁπάσας ἀναιρῶν. ἐν γάρ τοι τῇ γνώσει τῶν διαφορῶν ἑκάστου τῶν ὄντων αἱ τέχναι συνίστανται.
beads.english: So uneducated, then, is the argument Lycus propounds that he does not perceive that he is abolishing all the arts.

beads.greek: καὶ τοῦτο ἐπὶ πλεῖστον μὲν κἀν τῷ Φιλήβῳ διῆλθεν ὁ Πλάτων εὐθὺς ἐν ἀρχῇ τοῦ συγγράμματος· ἐφύλαξε δ’ αὐτοῦ τὴν γνώμην Ἀριστοτέλης καὶ Θεόφραστος, Χρύσιππός τε καὶ Μνησίθεος καὶ οὐδεὶς ὅστις οὐ διῆλθεν ἐν τῷ περὶ τέχνης γράμματι τὸν αὐτὸν λόγον.
beads.english: For it is in the knowledge of the differences of each of the things that are that the arts are constituted.

beads.greek: ἔστι δ’ ἡ μὲν πρώτη ῥῆσις ὑπὲρ τῆς κατὰ τὰς τέχνας συστάσεως τοῦ Πλάτωνος εἰρημένον τοιάδε. Σωκράτης.

τί μήν;
Σωκράτης.

The first passage of Plato concerning the constitution of the arts is stated as follows.
Socrates: ‘Sound, as it comes through the mouth, is for us one, I suppose, and again unlimited in multitude, both of all and of each.’ Protarchus: ‘What then?’ Socrates:

beads.greek: καὶ οὐδὲν ἑτέρων γε τούτων ἐσμέν πω σοφοὶ, οὔθ’ ὅτι τὸ ἄπειρον αὐτῆς ἴσμεν οὔθ’ ὅτι τὸ ἓν, ἀλλ’ ὅτι πόσα [210] τέ ἐστι καὶ ὁποῖα, τοῦτ’ ἔστι τὸ γραμματικὸν ἕκαστον ποιοῦν ἡμῶν; Πρώταρχος.
beads.english: ‘And we are not yet wise by either of these, neither because we know its unlimited nor because we know its one; but that we know how many [210] they are and of what sort, this is what makes each of us lettered.’ Protarchus: ‘Most true.’ Socrates: ‘And indeed what happens to make a man musical, this is the same thing.’ Protarchus: ‘How so?’ Socrates: ‘Sound, I suppose, is one in itself as regards that art too.’ Protarchus: ‘How could it not be?’ Socrates: ‘And let us posit two, low and high, and as a third the equal-toned; or how?’ Protarchus: ‘So.’ Socrates: ‘But you would not yet be wise in music knowing these things alone, while not knowing them you would be, so to speak, worth nothing in these matters.’ Protarchus: ‘Certainly not.’ Socrates:

beads.greek: ἀληθέστατα.
Σωκράτης.
καὶ μὴν καὶ τὸν μουσικὸν, ὃ τυγχάνει ποιοῦν, τοῦτ’ ἔστι ταὐτόν.
Πρώταρχος.
πῶς;
Σωκράτης.
φωνὴ μέν που τὸ κατ’ ἐκείνην τὴν τέχνην ἐστὶ μία μὲν αὐτῇ.
Πρώταρχος.
πῶς δὲ οὔ;
Σωκράτης.
δύο δὲ θῶμεν βαρὺ καὶ ὀξὺ καὶ τρίτονον ὁμότονον, ἢ πῶς;
Πρώταρχος.
οὕτως.
Σωκράτης.
ἀλλ’ οὔπω σοφὸς ἂν εἴης τὴν μουσικὴν εἰδὼς ταῦτα μόνα, μὴ εἰδὼς δὲ, ὥς γε ἔπος εἰπεῖν, εἰς ταῦτα οὐδενὸς ἄξιος ἔσῃ.
Πρώταρχος.
οὐ γὰρ οὖν.
Σωκράτης.

beads.greek: ἀλλ’ ὦ φίλε ἐπειδὰν λάβῃς τά τε διαστήματα ὁπόσα ἐστὶ τὸν ἀριθμὸν τῆς φωνῆς, ὀξύτητός τε περὶ καὶ βαρύτητος καὶ ὁποῖα καὶ τοὺς ὅρους τῶν διαστημάτων καὶ τὰ ἐκ τούτων ὅσα συστήματα γέγονεν, ἃ κατιδόντες οἱ πρόσθεν παρέδοσαν ἡμῖν τοῖς ἑπομένοις ἐκείνοις καλεῖν αὐτὰ ἁρμονίας, ἕν τε ταῖς κινήσεσιν αὖ τοῦ σώματος ἕτερα τοιαῦτα ἐνόντα πάθη γιγνόμενα, ἃ δι’ ἀριθμῶν μετρηθέντα, δεῖν αὐτά φησι ῥυθ μοὺς καὶ ﻿ [211] μέτρα ἐπονομάζειν καὶ ἅμα ἐννοεῖν, ὡς οὕτω δεῖ περὶ παντὸς ἑνὸς πολλῶν σκοπεῖν. ὅταν γὰρ αὐτὰ ταῦτά τε λάβῃς οὕτως, τότε ἐγένου σοφός.
beads.english: ‘But, my friend, when you have grasped the intervals of sound, how many they are in number, as regards highness and lowness, and of what sort, and the boundaries of the intervals, and how many systems have arisen out of these, which our predecessors discerned and handed down to us their followers, to call them harmoniai; and again that in the movements of the body there are other such affections coming to be, which, when measured by numbers, he says one must name rhythms and [211] metres, and at the same time to understand that this is how one must inquire about every one and many.

beads.greek: ὅταν δ’ ἄλλων τῶν ὄντων ὁτιοῦν ταύτῃ σκοπούμενος ἕλῃς, οὕτως ἔμφρων περὶ τούτου γέγονας. ἤρκει μὲν οὖν καὶ ταῦτα παρὰ Πλάτωνος ἀκοῦσαι τοῖς ἔχουσι νοῦν ἀκροαταῖς εἰς ἔνδειξιν ἁπασῶν τεχνῶν συστάσεως.

beads.greek: διαιρουμένῳ γὰρ τῷ Σωκράτει τὰς ἡδονὰς, ὁ διαλεγόμενος οὐ συνεχώρει διαφέρειν ἀλλήλων [212] ἁπάσας αὐτὰς, καθόσον εἰσὶν ἡδοναὶ, φάσκων ὁμοιοτάτας αὐτὰς ὑπάρχειν, ἀλλ’ ὅ γε Σωκράτης ἀπαντᾷ τῷ λόγῳ τῷδε. καὶ γὰρ χρῶμα, ὦ δαιμόνιε, χρώματι κατά γε αὐτὸ τοῦτο οὐδὲν διοίσει, τῷ χρῶμα εἶναι τὸ πᾶν.
beads.english: For when Socrates was dividing the pleasures, his interlocutor would not concede that they all differ from one another [212] insofar as they are pleasures, asserting that they are most alike; but Socrates meets him with this argument: ‘For indeed colour, my good sir, will in this very respect differ in nothing from colour, by the whole of it being colour; yet we all recognise that black, besides being different from white, is in fact also most opposite to it.

beads.greek: τό γε μὴν μέλαν τῷ λευκῷ πάντες γινώσκομεν ὡς πρὸς τῷ διάφορον εἶναι καὶ ἐναντιώτατον ὂν τυγχάνει. καὶ δὴ καὶ σχῆμα σχήματι, κατὰ ταὐτὸν γένει μέν ἐστι πᾶν ἕν.
beads.english: And so too figure with figure: in genus it is all one and the same; but of its parts, some are most opposite to one another, while others, I suppose, in fact have an infinite diversity.

beads.greek: τὰ δὲ μέρη τοῖς μέρεσιν αὐτοῦ τὰ μὲν ἐναντιώτατα ἀλλήλοις, τὰ δὲ διαφορότητα ἔχοντα μυρίαν που τυγχάνει.
καὶ πολλὰ ἕτερα οὕτως ἔχοντα εὑρήσομεν, ὥστε τούτῳ γε τῷ λόγῳ μὴ πίστευε τῷ πάντα τὰ ἐναντιώτατα ἓν ποιοῦντι. αὕτη μὲν ἡ περὶ χρωμάτων τε καὶ σχημάτων ῥῆσις.
beads.english: And we shall find many other things in this condition, so do not trust this argument which makes all the most opposite things one.’ This, then, is the passage about colours and figures.

english_sentences: For when Socrates was dividing the pleasures, his interlocutor would not concede that they all differ from one another [212] insofar as they are pleasures, asserting that they are most alike; but Socrates meets him with this argument: ‘For indeed colour, my good sir, will in this very respect differ in nothing from colour, by the whole of it being colour; yet we all recognise that black, besides being different from white, is in fact also most opposite to it.
And so too figure with figure: in genus it is all one and the same; but of its parts, some are most opposite to one another, while others, I suppose, in fact have an infinite diversity.
And we shall find many other things in this condition, so do not trust this argument which makes all the most opposite things one.’ This, then, is the passage about colours and figures.

beads.greek: ἡ δὲ περὶ τῶν ἡδονῶν ἥδε· ἥδεσθαι μέν φαμεν τὸν ἀκολασταίνοντα, ἥδεσθαι δὲ καὶ τὸν σωφρονοῦντα αὐτῷ τῷ σωφρονεῖν, ἥδεσθαι δ’ αὖ καὶ τὸν ἀνοηταίνοντα καὶ ἀνοήτων δοξῶν καὶ ἐλπίδων μεστὸν, ἥδεσθαι [213] δ’ αὖ καὶ τὸν φρονοῦντα αὐτῷ τῷ φρονεῖν, καὶ τούτων τῶν ἡδονῶν ἑκατέρας πῶς ἄν τις ὁμοίας ἀλλήλαις εἶναι λέγων οὐκ ἂν ἀνόητος φαίνοιτ’ ἂν ἐνδίκως; ὥσπερ δὲ τῶν ἡδονῶν τὰς διαφορὰς ὁ Πλάτων ἐν μὲν τῇδε τῇ ῥήσει διὰ βραχέων ἐνεδείξατο, καθ’ ὅλον δὲ τὸ βιβλίον ἐπὶ πλεῖον διῆλθεν, οὕτως τῶν τεχνῶν ἐν δυοῖν βιβλίοιν, τῷ Σοφιστῇ τε καὶ Πολιτικῷ.
beads.english: And the passage about pleasures is this: ‘We say that the licentious man takes pleasure, and that the temperate man too takes pleasure in the very fact of being temperate; and again that the foolish man, full of foolish opinions and hopes, takes pleasure, and again [213] that the wise man too takes pleasure in the very fact of being wise; and how could anyone who says that each of these pleasures is like the other not justly appear foolish?’ And just as Plato indicated the differences of pleasures briefly in this passage, but went through them at greater length through the whole book, so too those of the arts in two books, the Sophist and the Statesman.

beads.greek: ἆρ’ οὖν ἐπιστημῶν μὲν καὶ ἡδονῶν εἰσι διαφοραὶ πολλαὶ καὶ χρωμάτων καὶ σχημάτων καὶ τῶν ἐν ταῖς φωναῖς τόνων, ὡσαύτως δὲ καὶ ἡλικιῶν καὶ ὡρῶν καὶ χωρῶν καὶ νόσων, ἁπάντων τε τῶν ἄλλων, ἐν μόνοις δὲ τοῖς θερμοῖς ἤτοι γε οὐκ εἰσὶν ὅλως ἢ ἀδύνατος γιγνώσκεσθαι τοῖς ἀνθρώποις;
beads.english: Are there, then, many differences of sciences and of pleasures, and of colours and figures and of the pitches in sounds, and likewise too of ages and seasons and regions and diseases, and of all other things, but in hot things alone they either do not exist at all or are impossible for human beings to know?

beads.greek: καὶ μὴν ὅ γε τοῦ Λύκου λόγος ἀναιρεῖ τοῦ θερμοῦ τὰς διαφορὰς, ὡς οἴεται μὲν αὐτοῦ μόνου, κατὰ δὲ τὴν ἀλήθειαν, ἅμα τοῖς ἄλλοις ἅπασιν, εἴ γε ἡ τοῦ λόγου δύναμις ὁμοίως ἀντεπεκτείνασθαι δύναται.
beads.english: And indeed Lycus’ argument abolishes the differences of the hot, of it alone, as he thinks, but in truth, together with all the others, if indeed the force of the argument can be extended correspondingly in the same way.

beads.greek: καὶ γὰρ δὴ κἀπὶ τῶν ὑγρῶν αὐτῶν ἐφεξῆς ἐρῶ τάδε, μηδὲ ταῦτα διαφέρειν ἀλλήλων λέγων, καθόσον ὑγρά.
beads.english: For in fact I shall say the following next about moist things themselves as well, asserting that these too do not differ from one another insofar as they are moist.

beads.greek: τὸ δὲ δὴ μέγιστον αὐτοῦ τῶν ἁμαρτημάτων.
beads.english: But the very greatest of his errors is this.

beads.greek: ὅτι καὶ τὰς τέχνας ἁπάσας [214] ἀναιρεῖ τὴν σύστασιν ἐχούσας ἐν ταῖς τῶν εἰδῶν διαφοραῖς.
beads.english: That it also abolishes all the arts, [214] which have their constitution in the differences of the species.

beads.greek: ὁ μὲν οὖν Πλάτων ἐν κεφαλαίῳ γε προειπὼν ὑπὲρ τῆς τῶν τεχνῶν συστάσεως, ἐπὶ παραδείγματός τε διῆλθε τὸν λόγον, ἐπιδεικνὺς ὅπως ἡ γραμματικὴ συνέστη τέχνη, γνωσθείσης τῆς ἐν ταῖς φωναῖς διαφορᾶς.
beads.english: Plato, then, having first spoken in summary about the constitution of the arts, also went through the argument by way of an example, showing how the art of grammar was constituted once the difference in sounds had been recognised.

beads.greek: ὁ δὲ τοῦ Λύκου λόγος ἀναιρεῖ δηλονότι καὶ ταύτην τὴν τέχνην καὶ τὴν μουσικὴν ὁμοίως αὐτῇ καὶ τὰς ἀλλὰς ἁπάσας, ἀξιῶν τὸ ᾗ νενόηται, τὸ δέ τι μίαν ἔχειν ἐν αὐτῷ διαφοράν.
beads.english: But Lycus’ argument evidently abolishes this art too, and music likewise with it, and all the others, in requiring that the ‘insofar as it is conceived’ and the ‘in some respect’ have one difference in it.

beads.greek: θέασαι γοῦν ὅπως ἀναιρήσει πρώτην μὲν τὴν περὶ τὰ γράμματα τέχνην ὁ λόγος αὐτοῦ, μετὰ δὲ ταῦτα καὶ τὰς ἄλλας ἁπάσας. δοκεῖ μοι ἀδύνατον καὶ ἀμήχανον εἶναι τὴν φωνὴν ταύτην γε σκοποῦντι ᾗ νενόηται, κατ’ αὐτὴν λέγω τὴν ἐκφώνησιν, πρὸς ἑτέραν ἂν φωνὴν παραλλαγὴν ἔχειν, κατά τινα ἰδιότητα παραλλάττουσαν κατὰ ποιό τητα ἐν τῇ ἐκφωνήσει κειμένην.
beads.english: Observe, at any rate, how his argument will abolish first the art concerned with letters, and after this all the others as well: ‘It seems to me impossible and impracticable that sound, for one who considers this at least insofar as it is conceived, I mean in respect of the utterance itself, should have any variation with respect to another sound, varying according to some peculiarity in quality residing in the utterance.’

But Lycus’ argument evidently abolishes this art too, and music likewise with it, and all the others, in requiring that the ‘insofar as it is conceived’ and the ‘in some respect’ have one difference in it.

Observe, at any rate, how his argument will abolish first the art concerned with letters, and after this all the others as well: ‘It seems to me impossible and impracticable that sound, for one who considers this at least insofar as it is conceived, I mean in respect of the utterance itself, should have any variation with respect to another sound, varying according to some peculiarity in quality residing in the utterance.’

beads.greek: οὗτος ὁ λόγος αὐτός ἐστι πάντῃ τοῦ κατὰ τὴν ἀρχὴν γεγραμμένου τῆς ῥήσεως τῷ Λύκῳ καὶ δι’ αὐτῶν γε περαίνεται τῶν ἐκείνου ῥημάτων ἁπάντων ἑνὸς μόνου τοῦ κατὰ τὸ θερμὸν ὀνόματος εἰς τὸ τῆς φωνῆς [215] μεταβεβλημένου, ὥστ’ εἴπερ ἐκεῖνος ὑγιὴς, καὶ οὗτος· ἀλλὰ μὴν οὐχ ὑγιὴς οὗτος, ὥστ’ οὐδ’ ἐκεῖνος, εἰ μή τι ἄρα νομίζουσιν οἱ τὰ τοῦ Λύκου φρονοῦντες οὔτε τὴν ε φωνὴν ἑτέραν εἶναι τῆς ο, διαφέρειν δὲ τὴν ο τῆς ω.
beads.english: This argument is in every respect the same as the one written by Lycus at the beginning of his passage, and it is carried through by means of those very words of his, all of them, with only one, the name of ‘hot’, changed into that of ‘sound’; [215] so that if that one is valid, so too is this; but surely this one is not valid, so that neither is that one, unless perhaps those who hold Lycus’ views think that neither is the sound e different from o, nor does o differ from ō.

beads.greek: εἰ δὲ καὶ ταύτας ἑτέρας ἀλλήλων ὁμολογήσομεν εἶναι καὶ πρὸς ταῦτα καὶ τὴν α καὶ τὴν ι καὶ τὴν υ. καὶ τῶν ἄλλων ἁπάντων γραμμάτων, αὗται μὲν ἔσονται τέτταρες ἐπὶ ταῖς εἴκοσιν.
beads.english: But if we shall agree that these too are different from one another, and in addition to these a and i and u, and all the other letters, these will be twenty-four in number.

beads.greek: ἡ γνοῦσα δ’ αὐτῶν τὴν διαφορὰν τέχνη γραμματικὴ, καθάπερ γε καὶ μουσικὴ τέχνη περὶ τὴν ἐν ταῖς φωναῖς ὀξύτητα καὶ βαρύτητα, καίτοι καὶ ταύτας οὐδὲν ἧττον ὁ τοῦ Λύκου λόγος ἀναιρεῖ.
beads.english: And the art that knows their difference is grammar, just as the art of music too concerns the highness and lowness in sounds; and yet Lycus’ argument abolishes these no less.

beads.greek: φωνὴ γὰρ φωνῆς, ᾗ φωνὴ, διαφέρειν οὐδὲν, ἀλλ’ ὅμως ὁ μὲν τῆς μέσης φθόγγος ὀξύτερος μέν ἐστι τόνῳ τῆς λιχανοῦ τῶν μέσων, βαρύτερος δὲ τόνῳ τῆς παραμέσης.
beads.english: For sound differs in nothing from sound insofar as it is sound; but nonetheless the note of the mese is higher by a tone than that of the lichanos of the mesai, and lower by a tone than that of the paramese.

beads.greek: αὐτῶν δ’ ἐκείνων πάλιν ὁ μὲν τῆς λιχανοῦ τῆς παρυπάτου τῶν μέσων ὀξύτερος τόνῳ. ὁ δὲ τῆς παραμέσης βαρυτέρως ἡμιτόνῳ τῆς τρίτης τῶν διεζευγμένων.
beads.english: And of those in turn, the note of the lichanos is higher by a tone than that of the parhypate of the mesai; while that of the paramese is lower by a semitone than that of the trite of the diezeugmenai.

ὁ δὲ τῆς παραμέσης βαρυτέρως ἡμιτόνῳ τῆς τρίτης τῶν διεζευγμένων.

beads.english: Then again others higher and lower than those, and then again others than those, until we arrive at the highest and the lowest [216] note of all.

beads.greek: ἀλλ’ ὁ θαυμασιώτατος Λύκος οὐκ αἰσθάνεται ταῦτα πάντα ἀναιρῶν ἐν τῷ λέγειν· δοκεῖ μοι ἀδύνατον καὶ ἀμήχανον εἶναι τὸ θερμὸν ταῦτά γε σκοποῦντι, ᾗ νενόηται, κατ’ αὐτὴν λέγω τὴν θάλψιν, πρὸς ἕτερον αὖθις παραλλαγὴν ἔχειν. καλὸν εἰ μηδὲ χρῶμα χρώματος, ᾗ χρῶμά ἐστι, διαφέρειν εἰπὼν, ἀναιρεῖ τὴν γραφικὴν τέχνην, ἐρυθρόν γέ τι παραθεμένην χρῶμα καὶ λευκὸν καὶ μέλαν καὶ ξανθὸν, ὅσα τ’ ἄλλα τοιαῦτα.

But the most admirable Lycus does not perceive that he abolishes all these things when he says: ‘It seems to me impossible and impracticable, at least to one considering these matters, that the hot, in the respect in which it is conceived — I mean in respect of the warming itself — should again have any variation relative to another.’ It would be a fine thing if, by saying that colour too does not differ from colour, insofar as it is colour, he also abolished the art of painting, which sets side by side some red colour and white and black and yellow, and all the other such colours.

For surely his argument is far more persuasive when stated about colours as well than as it has now been stated about the hot; for we say that hot differs from hot, yet not that it is in every way its contrary, whereas colour not only differs from colour, but black is also in its very nature the most contrary of all to white.

beads.greek: [217] Καὶ πῶς ἐγχωρεῖ, φήσειεν ἂν ὁ Λύκος, ἐναντίον εἶναι τῷ χρώματι καθ’ ὃ νενόηται χρῶμα ὄν; καὶ ἀληθεύσει γε ναὶ μὰ τοὺς θεοὺς, ὅσον ἐπὶ χρώματος καὶ τὸ χρῶμα μηδὲν ἡγούμενος ἕτερον ἑτέρου διαφέρειν, ἀλλ’ ὥσπερ τοῦτο ἀληθὲς, οὕτω κἀκεῖνο τὸ λευκὸν τοῦ μέλανος οὐ μόνον διαφέρον, ἀλλὰ καὶ τοσοῦτον διαφέρον, ὡς ἐναντιώτατον εἶναι.

beads.greek: καὶ πῶς ἐγχωρεῖ, τάχα φήσουσιν οἱ τὰ τοῦ Λύκου πρεσβεύοντες, ἅμα μὲν εἶναι ταὐτὸν, ἅμα δὲ ἐναντιώτατον εἶναι; καὶ πῶς τῷ μέλανι λευκόν;
beads.english: And how can white be so to black?’ To whom we shall answer only this much: that if it is not possible for white to be at once both contrary to black and the same as it, let them choose one of the two.

beads.greek: οἷς ἡμεῖς ἀποκρινούμεθά τί γε τοσοῦτον, ὡς εἴπερ οὐκ ἐγχωρεῖ τὸ λευκὸν ἐναντίον τε ἅμα καὶ ταὐτὸν εἶναι τῷ μέλανι, τὸ ἕτερον αὐτοῦ αἱρείσθωσαν. ὁ μὲν γὰρ Πλάτων οἴεται δυνατὸν εἶναι, καθάπερ γε καὶ Ἀριστοτέλης καὶ Θεόφραστος, ἕτερον ἑτέρω ταὐτὸν ὂν τῷ γένει, τοσαύτην ὅμως ἔχειν τὴν ἐν εἴδει διαφορὰν, ὡς ἐναντιώτατον ὑπάρχειν.
beads.english: For Plato thinks it possible, as indeed do Aristotle and Theophrastus, that one thing, while being the same as another in genus, nevertheless has so great a difference in species as to be its most complete contrary.

beads.greek: οὗτοι δ’ εἰ μὴ νομίζουσιν ἀληθεύειν ἄμφω τὸν λόγον τὸν ἐναργέστερον ἑλέσθωσαν.
beads.english: But if these men do not think that both statements are true, let them choose the more evident one.

beads.greek: [218] ἐναργέστερον δέ ἐστιν, ὅσῳ καὶ πᾶσιν ἀνθρώποις ὁμολογούμενον, ἐναντίον εἶναι τὸ λευκὸν τῷ μέλανι.
beads.english: [218] And the more evident one is that white is contrary to black, inasmuch as this is also agreed by all men.

beads.greek: καὶ μὴν, εἵπερ ἀληθές ἐστι τοῦτο, νομίζουσι δὲ αὐτοὶ μὴ δύνασθαι τοὺς λόγους ἀμφοτέρους ἀληθεύεσθαι, τόν τε ἐναντίον εἶναι φάσκοντα τὸ λευκὸν τῷ μέλανι καὶ τὸν αὐτὸν οὐκ ὀρθῶς ἐροῦσιν μηδὲν διαφέρειν ᾗ χρῶμά ἐστιν τὸ λευκὸν τοῦ μέλανος. ὁ μὲν οὖν ἐν τῷ τοῦ Πλάτωνος γράμματι διαλεγόμενος τῷ Σωκράτει, συγγνωστὸς ἦν ἴσως, κωλύων τὸν Σωκράτην διαιρούμενον ἡδονὴν ἡδονῆς διαφορᾷ.

beads.greek: οὐ γὰρ ἦν που βιβλίον οὐδὲν τοιοῦτο διδάσκων, ὡς ἐγχωρεῖ πολλὰ πολλοῖς ὄντα τῷ γένει ταὐτὰ διαφέρειν ὅμως εἰς τοσοῦτον, ὡς ἐναντιώτατον ἀλλήλοις ἰδέαν τε καὶ φύσιν ἔχειν. ἐπεὶ δ’ ὑπὸ Πλάτωνος ὁ Φίληβος ἐγράφη διδάσκων τἀληθὲς, εἰ μὲν οὐδ’ ὅλως ἀνέγνω τὸ βιβλίον ὁ Λύκος, ἄγαμαι τῆς παιδείας τὸν Λύκον.

beads.greek: εἰ δ’ ἀναγνοὺς οὐκ ἐνόησε, θαυμάζω τῆς συνέσεως. εἰ δὲ νοήσας οὐκ ἐπείσθη, μακαρίζω τῆς κρίσεως.

beads.greek: ὦ πρὸς τοῦ Διὸς ἐρωτᾷ τίς λόγον οὐδὲ τὰ [219] πρῶτα μαθὼν τῆς διαλεκτικῆς;
beads.english: O, by Zeus, does someone propound an argument who has not learned even the [219] first elements of dialectic?

beads.greek: ἔστι τίς ἂν ἄνθρωπος Ἕλλην ἰατρὸς ἢ γραμματικὸς ἢ ῥήτωρ ἢ φιλόσοφος ἢ ὅλως ὁστισοῦν ἄλλος ἀντιποιούμενος λόγων, ὡς οὐκ ἀνέγνω τὸν Πλάτωνος Φίληβον;
beads.english: Could there be any Greek man — physician or grammarian or rhetor or philosopher, or in general anyone else at all who lays claim to argument — who has not read Plato’s Philebus?

beads.greek: καίτοι τί λέγω τὸν Φίληβον;
beads.english: And yet why do I speak of the Philebus?

beads.greek: οὐ γὰρ ἐν τούτῳ μόνῳ τὸν προκείμενον λόγον Πλάτων ἐδίδαξεν, ἀλλὰ καὶ δι’ ἄλλων πολλῶν ἐπεμνήσθη βιβλίων, ὧν ἐχρῆν μόνον κἂν ἕν γέ τι τὸν θαυμασιώτατον Λύκον ἀνεγνωκέναι, ἀντιποιούμενον λόγων ἐπιστημονικῶν.
beads.english: For it was not in this work alone that Plato taught the argument in question, but he mentioned it also in many other books, of which the most admirable Lycus ought to have read at least some one, since he lays claim to scientific arguments.

beads.greek: αἰσχρὸν γὰρ Ἱπποκράτην διελέγχειν ἐπιχειροῦντα καὶ λόγους ἐπερωτῶντα περαντικοὺς, ὡς νομίζει, μηδὲ τὰ πρῶτα φαίνεσθαι μεμαθηκότα τῶν ἐν ταῖς φιλοσόφων διατριβαῖς.
beads.english: For it is shameful that one who undertakes to refute Hippocrates and who propounds arguments that are, as he thinks, conclusive, should appear not to have learned even the first elements of what is taught in the schools of the philosophers.

beads.greek: ἀλλὰ νὴ Διὰ θαυμαστὸν αὐτοῦ τὸ περὶ τῶν ὑγρῶν ἐστι παράδειγμα.
beads.english: But, by Zeus, his example concerning liquids is a marvel.

beads.greek: καὶ γὰρ τοῦτο βούλεται, μηδὲν ἀλλήλων διηφέρειν, εἰ πάντα ἐστὶν ὑγρὰ, καθ’ ὃ μέντοι τὰ μὲν ὀξέα, τὰ δὲ στρυφνὰ, τὰ δ’ ἁλμυρὰ, τὰ δὲ γλυκέα, ταύτῃ διαλλάττει, οὐκ ἀκούει δὲ ἐν τούτοις αὐτὸς ἑαυτοῦ.
beads.english: For this too is what he means: that they do not differ from one another at all, if all are liquids; but in the respect in which some are sour, some astringent, some salty, and some sweet, in this respect they do differ — and here he does not listen to himself.

beads.greek: ἔοικεν οὖν ὡς ἀπίου καὶ μεσπίλου καὶ μήλου καὶ κυδωνίου τοῦ ὄξους αἰσθάνεσθαι, καίτοι γε πάντων ἀνθρώπων ἔνια μὲν τῶν μήλων ﻿ [221] ὀξέα καλούντων, ἔνια δὲ στύφοντα, γλυκέα δὲ ἄλλα, καθάπερ, οἶμαι, καὶ ῥοιὰς ὀξείας τε καὶ στυφούσας καὶ γλυκείας.
beads.english: He seems, then, to perceive vinegar as he does pear and medlar and apple and quince, although all men call some apples [221] sour, others styptic, and yet others sweet, just as, I think, they also call pomegranates sour and styptic and sweet.

beads.greek: ἐν μέν γε τοῖς οἴνοις, ᾧ ἀρετὴ κακίας ἀφώρισται, στύψις ὀξύτητος, εὐγενεῖς μὲν γὰρ οἱ στύφοντες. ὀξὺς δ’ οὐδεὶς κατὰ φύσιν, ἀλλ’ εἰ καὶ μικρὸν αὐτοῖς προσέλθῃ τοιαύτης ποιότητος, ὑποπτεύομεν αὐτίκα τὴν εἰς ὄξος αὐτῶν μεταβολήν.
beads.english: In wines, at any rate, that by which excellence is marked off from badness is stypticity from sourness; for the styptic wines are of noble quality, whereas none is sour by nature, but if even a little of such a quality comes upon them, we at once suspect their change into vinegar.

beads.greek: ἴσως οὖν ὁ Λύκος οὐδ’ ὀξυλάπαθον, οὐδ’ ὀξυαλίδα, λαπάθου τε καὶ θριδακίνης διεγίνωσκεν, οἷς στυφούσης μὲν ποιότητος οὐδὲ τοὐλάχιστον ὑπάρχει, τῆς δὲ ὀξείας δαψιλῶς μετέσχηκεν ἄμφω.
beads.english: Perhaps, then, Lycus did not even distinguish sour dock (oxylapathon) or sorrel (oxyalis) from dock and lettuce — plants in which there is not the least trace of the styptic quality, while both have a plentiful share of the sour.

beads.greek: θαυμαστὸν μὲν οὖν εἰ ταῦτα μὲν ἀπὸ τῆς ὀξείας ποιότητος ὠνόμασται, τὸ δὲ ὄξος αὐτὸ οὐ μετέσχηκεν αὐτῆς.
beads.english: It would be surprising indeed if these are named after the sour quality, while vinegar itself has no share in it.

beads.greek: ἀλλ’ ὁ μηδὲ τὰς κοινὰς αἰσθήσεις ἀποσώζων Λύκος, ἐγκαλεῖν Ἱπποκράτει τολμᾷ.
beads.english: But Lycus, who does not preserve even the common senses, dares to bring charges against Hippocrates.

beads.greek: πάλιν οὖν ἔγνω τὴν παρὰ τοῖς φυσικοῖς ζήτησιν ὑπὲρ τοῦ τῶν χυμῶν ἀριθμοῦ.
beads.english: Again, then, he was acquainted with the inquiry among the natural philosophers about the number of flavours.

beads.greek: κατὰ τοῦτο γὰρ οὐδὲν, ὡς ἔοικε, διαφέρει χυμὸς χυμοῦ, καθόσον χυμός ἐστιν.
beads.english: For in this respect, as it seems, flavour does not differ from flavour, insofar as it is flavour.

greek_sentences: ἔοικεν οὖν ὡς ἀπίου καὶ μεσπίλου καὶ μήλου καὶ κυδωνίου τοῦ ὄξους αἰσθάνεσθαι, καίτοι γε πάντων ἀνθρώπων ἔνια μὲν τῶν μήλων ﻿ [221] ὀξέα καλούντων, ἔνια δὲ στύφοντα, γλυκέα δὲ ἄλλα, καθάπερ, οἶμαι, καὶ ῥοιὰς ὀξείας τε καὶ στυφούσας καὶ γλυκείας.
ἐν μέν γε τοῖς οἴνοις, ᾧ ἀρετὴ κακίας ἀφώρισται, στύψις ὀξύτητος, εὐγενεῖς μὲν γὰρ οἱ στύφοντες.
ὀξὺς δ’ οὐδεὶς κατὰ φύσιν, ἀλλ’ εἰ καὶ μικρὸν αὐτοῖς προσέλθῃ τοιαύτης ποιότητος, ὑποπτεύομεν αὐτίκα τὴν εἰς ὄξος αὐτῶν μεταβολήν.
ἴσως οὖν ὁ Λύκος οὐδ’ ὀξυλάπαθον, οὐδ’ ὀξυαλίδα, λαπάθου τε καὶ θριδακίνης διεγίνωσκεν, οἷς στυφούσης μὲν ποιότητος οὐδὲ τοὐλάχιστον ὑπάρχει, τῆς δὲ ὀξείας δαψιλῶς μετέσχηκεν ἄμφω.
θαυμαστὸν μὲν οὖν εἰ ταῦτα μὲν ἀπὸ τῆς ὀξείας ποιότητος ὠνόμασται, τὸ δὲ ὄξος αὐτὸ οὐ μετέσχηκεν αὐτῆς.
ἀλλ’ ὁ μηδὲ τὰς κοινὰς αἰσθήσεις ἀποσώζων Λύκος, ἐγκαλεῖν Ἱπποκράτει τολμᾷ.
πάλιν οὖν ἔγνω τὴν παρὰ τοῖς φυσικοῖς ζήτησιν ὑπὲρ τοῦ τῶν χυμῶν ἀριθμοῦ.
κατὰ τοῦτο γὰρ οὐδὲν, ὡς ἔοικε, διαφέρει χυμὸς χυμοῦ, καθόσον χυμός ἐστιν.
english_sentences: He seems, then, to perceive vinegar as he does pear and medlar and apple and quince, although all men call some apples [221] sour, others styptic, and yet others sweet, just as, I think, they also call pomegranates sour and styptic and sweet.

In wines, at any rate, that by which excellence is marked off from badness is stypticity from sourness; for the styptic wines are of noble quality, whereas none is sour by nature, but if even a little of such a quality comes upon them, we at once suspect their change into vinegar.

Perhaps, then, Lycus did not even distinguish sour dock (oxylapathon) or sorrel (oxyalis) from dock and lettuce — plants in which there is not the least trace of the styptic quality, while both have a plentiful share of the sour.
It would be surprising indeed if these are named after the sour quality, while vinegar itself has no share in it.
But Lycus, who does not preserve even the common senses, dares to bring charges against Hippocrates.
Again, then, he was acquainted with the inquiry among the natural philosophers about the number of flavours.
For in this respect, as it seems, flavour does not differ from flavour, insofar as it is flavour.

beads.greek: ἡδέως ἂν οὖν ἤκουσα τίνος τῶν ὄντων εἰσὶν αἱ τοιαῦται διαφοραὶ, γλυκὺς, ὀξὺς, δριμὺς, [222] πικρὸς, ἁλμυρὸς, ἀλυκὸς, στρυφνὸς, αὐστηρὸς, στύφων, λιπαρός.
beads.english: I should gladly have heard, then, of what among existing things such differences are — sweet, sour, pungent, [222] bitter, briny, salty, astringent, harsh, styptic, oily.

beads.greek: εἰ μὴ γὰρ χυμῶν ἴσως ἤτοι φωνῶν ἢ χρωμάτων ἢ ὀδμῶν ἢ διὰ τῆς ἁφῆς εἰς γνῶσιν ἥκουσι. παρὰ ταύτας γὰρ οὐκ ἔχομεν ἄλλην αἴσθησιν.
beads.english: For if they are not differences of flavours, they perhaps come to be known either as differences of sounds or of colours or of odours, or through touch; for besides these we have no other sense.

beads.greek: ἀλλ’ εἰσὶν αἱ πᾶσαι πέντε, γεῦσις καὶ ἀκοὴ καὶ ὄψις καὶ ὄσφρησίς τε καὶ ἁφή.
beads.english: But they are five in all: taste and hearing and sight and smell and touch.

beads.greek: διαγινώσκομεν δὲ ὥσπερ καὶ ταῖς ἄλλαις ἄλλα τῶν αἰσθητῶν, οὕτως τῇ γεύσει καὶ τοὺς χυμούς.
beads.english: And just as we discern other sensible objects by the other senses, so we discern flavours too by taste.

beads.greek: ὡς δὲ ἐν τοῖς ὑγροῖς αἱ διαφοραὶ πολλαὶ, κατὰ τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον κἀν ταῖς αἰσθήσεσιν.
beads.english: And as the differences among liquids are many, in the same way so are they among the senses too.

beads.greek: καίτοι γε ᾗ αἰσθήσεις εἰσὶν, οὐ διαφέρουσιν, ἀλλ’ ὁ διαλεκτικώτατος Λύκος οὐκ ἐάσει λέγειν ἡμᾶς οὔτ’ ἐν τοῖς χυμοῖς εἶναι τὰς εἰρημένας διαφορὰς, οὐδὲ ἐν ταῖς αἰσθήσεσιν, ἃς ἅπαντες γιγνώσκουσιν, οὔτ’ ἐν τοῖς χρώμασι καὶ λευκὸν καὶ μέλαν καὶ φαιὸν καὶ ξανθὸν καὶ πυῤῥὸν, ἐρυθρόν τε καὶ φοινικοῦν καὶ κυανοῦν.
beads.english: And yet, insofar as they are senses, they do not differ; but the most dialectical Lycus will not allow us to say either that the differences mentioned exist in flavours, or in the senses — differences which everyone recognises — or in colours: white and black and grey and yellow and tawny, red and crimson and dark blue.

beads.greek: οὔτε γὰρ χρῶμα χρώματος ᾗ χρῶμά ἐστι διαφέρει.
beads.english: For colour does not differ from colour insofar as it is colour.

beads.greek: μαίνονται τοίνυν ἅπαντες ἰατροὶ καὶ φιλόσοφοι χρωμάτων μὲν ἡγούμενοι διαφορὰς εἶναι τὰς εἰρημένας.
beads.english: All physicians and philosophers are therefore mad in holding that the differences mentioned are differences of colours,

ἀλλ’ εἰσὶν αἱ πᾶσαι πέντε, γεῦσις καὶ ἀκοὴ καὶ ὄψις καὶ ὄσφρησίς τε καὶ ἁφή.
